We begin with bodies from everyday life: the floor of a storey, a trench cover, the sheet metal of a car body, the wing of an aircraft. All are flat and have one dimension, the thickness, much smaller than the other two. In 5 we treated slender bodies and described them by a function of one variable, the deflection of the axis. Here only one dimension is small, so we must write equilibrium, energy and vibration for two dimensions at once.

In everyday language the word plate (plošča) means a flat, thin piece. Engineers use it for a flat body that is thin compared with its other two dimensions and is loaded perpendicular to its plane. A plate is therefore distinguished from a shell (lupina), which is just as thin but curved. As a beam is described by its axis, a plate is described by the plane halfway through its thickness.

Why this matters is shown by a steel plate with a square plan of side \(500\) mm and thickness \(10\) mm, which accompanies all the calculations of the chapter. Under a load of \(10\) kPa it bends a little more than a tenth of a millimetre at its centre, and its lowest natural frequency is about \(190\) Hz. The first figure decides whether a floor or a cover carries the load, the second whether a machine turning at a similar frequency excites the plate. If we compress the plate in its own plane it can buckle, and the chapter shows at which load.

The chapter promises three things. First, from the assumptions about a thin plate we derive, following the beam, the displacements, the internal forces, a single equation of equilibrium and the edge conditions of the different supports. Second, we solve the equation on a strip, on a rectangle with the series of 13 and on a circular plate, and then use energy methods to find vibration and buckling. Third, we show where the simplification fails for thick plates and carry the plate over to the finite elements of 12.

18.1 The Kirchhoff plate

The beam of chapter 5 is a slender body: one measure, the length, is much larger than the other two, and so we describe it by a function of one variable, the deflection of its axis. A surface structure has one measure, the thickness, much smaller than the other two (section 5.1.1). If it is flat, we call it a plate (plošča). The floor of a storey, the cover of a ditch, the sheet metal of a car body and the wing of an aircraft are plates. We ask the same question as for the beam, now for two dimensions. How do we describe a plate by a function of two variables, how do its points move, which forces does a cross-section of the plate carry, and what is the stress that belongs to these forces? This section answers these questions. From them we shall derive, in the rest of the chapter, the equation that determines the deflection.

One example accompanies all the calculations: a steel plate with a square plan of side \(a = 500\) mm and thickness \(h = 10\) mm. The material is the steel of the book, \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) (section 3.1.2). The plate is thus fifty times wider than it is thick, \(a/h = 50\). The load \(q = 10\) kPa, a force of \(10\,000\) N on every square metre, will be introduced in the next section. All results of the chapter are linear in the load.

18.1.1 The plate

Let us draw what we are talking about (figure 18.1). For visibility we drew the thickness far too large, in reality \(h/a = 0{,}02\).

We start with two parallel planes, the upper and the lower, set apart by the thickness \(h\). The body between them is the plate, bounded in plan by its sides. The plane halfway between them is the middle plane, drawn dashed. In it we place the axes: \(x\) and \(y\) lie in the middle plane, \(z\) is perpendicular to it and points up. The triple stays right-handed, as in the earlier chapters, and \(z\) is the same direction as \(y\) for the beam, where we measured the height upwards. The plan has measures \(a\) and \(b\), the thickness is \(h\). The name comes from everyday speech: a plate is something flat, that is thin and wide, like a stone slab or a plate on the floor. We choose the middle plane because the stresses, as the theorem below will show, are odd functions of the height \(z\) above it.

Definition 18.1 Plate (plošča)

Let \(\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) be a bounded open set of the plane \(xy\) whose boundary consists of finitely many smooth curves, and let \(h > 0\) be a number. A plate is the body

\[P = \{ (x, y, z) : (x, y) \in \Omega,\ -h/2 \le z \le h/2 \} . \tag{18.1}\]

The set \(\Omega\) is the middle plane (srednja ravnina) of the plate, taken as the set of points with \(z = 0\), the number \(h\) is the thickness (debelina), the planes \(z = \pm h/2\) are the faces (ploskvi), and \(\partial\Omega \times [-h/2, h/2]\) is the edge of the plate. By \(a\) we denote a characteristic measure of the plan: for a rectangle the shorter side, for a circle the radius (the sources measure the diameter, so for a circle our limit is twice as strict as theirs). The plate is thin if \(h/a \le 0{,}05\). It is loaded by a load perpendicular to the middle plane and by forces and moments on the edge.

Source: VK (PDF p. 6) describes a plate as a flat structure between two parallel planes with a small thickness against the other measures, and the load mostly perpendicular to it. The limit of a thin plate \(h/a \le 0{,}05\) is in ONATE2 (PDF p. 268), \(t/L \le 0{,}05\). EP (p. 392) writes that a plate is thin if the ratio of thickness to the smallest in-plane measure is \(20\) or more, which is a misprint: at a ratio of thickness to measure of \(20\) the plate would be thicker than it is wide. The meaning EP intends is \(a/h \ge 20\) and it coincides with the limit \(h/a \le 0{,}05\) when \(a\) is the smallest in-plane measure. ONATE2 measures \(L\) as the average side, which for a square is the same measure. For a circle the smallest measure is the diameter, while our \(a\) is the radius, so for a circle our limit is stricter than both sources.

We took the limit \(h/a \le 0{,}05\) from two sources and explain it in the part on idealizations below. Our plate satisfies it with room to spare: \(h/a = 0{,}02\), that is \(a/h = 50\). The beam of chapter 5 has thus become flat in this chapter: there \(h\) was the height of the cross-section, small against the length, here it is small against both measures of the plan.

18.1.2 Kirchhoff idealizations and the displacement field

For the beam we used the model of Euler and Bernoulli: cross-sections stay plane and perpendicular to the axis (definition 5.14). We use the same idea for the plate, where what stays straight is a straight line perpendicular to the middle plane. We call it the normal (normala) of the middle plane: the segment \(\{(x, y, z) : |z| \le h/2\}\) at constant \(x\), \(y\) (normal in figure 18.2).

Look at figure 18.2. Grey is the plate before loading: the middle plane is dashed, the axis \(x\) horizontal, \(z\) up. The point \(A\) on the middle plane and the point \(B\) above it on the upper face lie on the same normal. After bending the middle plane curves into the curve \(z = w(x)\), the faces curve with it, and the normal stays a straight line perpendicular to the curved middle plane. It therefore rotates through an angle equal to the slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the middle plane (for a small slope, as we had for the beam). The point \(B\) therefore moves horizontally by the distance \(z\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) towards smaller \(x\), where \(z\) is the height of the point above the middle plane, and vertically by \(w\). These are the displacements that we write down in the theorem below.

Before we write them down, we must say what we demand of the model. For the beam we listed the conditions in a definition, and here we do the same.

Definition 18.2 Kirchhoff plate (Kirchhoffova plošča)

Let the plate \(P\) of definition 18.1 be made of a homogeneous, isotropic, linearly elastic material with modulus of elasticity \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\), \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) (definitions 3.1 and 3.2). A Kirchhoff plate has five idealizations.

  1. It is thin: \(h/a \le 0{,}05\).
  2. Deflections are small: the displacement of a point of the middle plane in the direction \(z\), the deflection \(w(x, y)\), is at most \(h/5\) in absolute value, and the square of the slope is small, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 \le 10^{-2}\).
  3. Normals stay straight and perpendicular to the middle plane and keep their length: at interior points of the plate \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).
  4. The middle plane does not move in its own plane: \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) at \(z = 0\).
  5. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is zero, every layer \(z = \text{constant}\) is in a plane stress state (definition 11.32), and its in-plane strains follow from Hooke's law (theorem 3.11) with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\).

Source: VK (PDF pp. 12-13) lists six Kirchhoff assumptions, of which our 1, 3, 4 and 5 are the same (VK 4: straight normals of preserved length, VK 5: the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is neglected, VK 6: the middle plane stays unstretched). Assumption 2 is only qualitative in VK (small deflections), and the limits \(h/5\) and \(10^{-2}\) we derive below. ONATE2 (PDF pp. 267-268) says that the condition of straight and perpendicular normals holds only for thin plates. EP (pp. 427-428) combines the assumptions into the displacement field (7.2.78) for pure bending.

Let us name what these idealizations mean. The first says that the plate is much wider than it is thick, so that a straight line across the thickness can be treated as a normal of the middle plane at all: the thicker the plate, the more the normal distorts (ONATE2 PDF p. 268, \(0{,}05 \le t/L < 0{,}10\) is a moderately thick plate and \(t/L \ge 0{,}10\) a very thick one). The third is the same conclusion as for the beam: the model describes the deformation across the thickness by three numbers, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(w\), instead of an unknown function. The fifth says what still carries stress: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which are linear in \(z\), as we shall see. The idealizations are only an approximation and we shall test them with numbers at the end of the section.

By the third idealization we neglect the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) in the deformation, but they are not zero: the transverse shear forces need them (section 18.2). The Euler-Bernoulli beam had the same contradiction (section 5.3.4). The way out is the same: we get the stress from equilibrium, not from Hooke's law.

Theorem 18.3 Displacement field of a plate (polje pomikov plošče)

Let the plate \(P\) be a Kirchhoff plate (definition 18.2) and let its displacement field \((u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) have continuous partial derivatives of first and second order at interior points of the plate. Then there is a function \(w(x, y)\) on \(\Omega\) with continuous partial derivatives up to second order such that at every interior point of the plate

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = w(x, y) , \tag{18.2}\]

where the index denotes a partial derivative (\(w_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial w/\partial x\)). The nonzero strain components are

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{yy}} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{xy}} . \tag{18.3}\]
Proof

We must show that \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) does not depend on \(z\), that \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) depend linearly on \(z\) with coefficients \(-w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(-w_{\mathrm{y}}\), and that the strains follow from this. We use corollary 1.85 on a function with zero derivative, on segments in the interior of the plate along lines parallel to the axis \(z\), as in the proof of theorem 5.15.

  1. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = 0\) (idealization 3), by corollary 1.85 on the segment from \((x, y, 0)\) to \((x, y, z)\), it follows that \(u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) = u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, 0) =: w(x, y)\). The function \(w\) is the restriction of \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) to the plane \(z = 0\) and so has continuous derivatives up to second order.
  2. Since \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = w(x, y)\) for every \(z\), we have \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) at every point. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = 0\) (equation (1.63), idealization 3) it follows that \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = -w_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y)\).
  3. The function \(u_{\mathrm{x}} + z\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) has the derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) with respect to \(z\). By corollary 1.85 it is therefore equal to its value at \(z = 0\), that is \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, 0) = 0\) (idealization 4). Hence \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). In the same way \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) gives \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  4. We get the strains from equation (1.63): \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = -z\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x) = -\tfrac12 z\,(w_{\mathrm{xy}} + w_{\mathrm{yx}}) = -z\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}\), because the mixed derivatives are equal (theorem 8.30). The components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are zero by idealization 3.
  5. Rotation of the normal: by definition 1.116, \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z - \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x) = -w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and similarly \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = -w_{\mathrm{y}}\). The size of the rotation of the normal is therefore the slope of the middle plane, as figure 18.2 shows.

Source: EP (7.2.78), (7.2.79) (p. 428), VK (2.1)-(2.6) (PDF pp. 22-24), ONATE2 (5.5), (5.7) (PDF pp. 267-268). VK writes \(w\) positive downwards, so the displacements in VK (2.2) have the opposite sign, but are the same in substance.

Idealization 2 now has its meaning. We need the deflection \(w \le h/5\) and the slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 \le 10^{-2}\) so that the middle plane is really unstretched (idealization 4). How well this holds, we test on the example. Let the plate be simply supported along its edges (the points of the edges cannot move sideways) and bend into \(w = w_0 \sin(\pi x/a)\). Then the middle plane stretches, because the curve is longer than its chord: the stretch of a longitudinal line is about \(\tfrac12 w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\), which averaged over \(x\) becomes \(\tfrac14 (\pi w_0/a)^2\). The bending strain on the face is by equation (18.3) \(\tfrac h2\,w_0\,(\pi/a)^2\). The ratio of the two is \(w_0/(2h)\). For our plate with \(w_0 = 0{,}014\,h\) (\(w_0 = 0{,}14\) mm, the deflection of the centre of the square in section 18.5) the ratio is \(0{,}007\) or \(0{,}7\) %. For larger deflections we compute the ratio in the table (NumPy, the ratio is exactly \(w_0/(2h)\)). The columns are: the deflection of the centre \(w_0\) in units of \(h\), the largest slope, the mean stretch of the middle plane, the bending strain of the face and the ratio of the two.

\(w_0/h\) largest slope \(\pi w_0/a\) mean stretch of the middle plane bending strain of the face ratio
\(0{,}014\) \(8{,}8\cdot 10^{-4}\) \(1{,}93\cdot 10^{-7}\) \(2{,}76\cdot 10^{-5}\) \(0{,}007\)
\(0{,}1\) \(6{,}3\cdot 10^{-3}\) \(9{,}87\cdot 10^{-6}\) \(1{,}97\cdot 10^{-4}\) \(0{,}05\)
\(0{,}2\) \(1{,}3\cdot 10^{-2}\) \(3{,}95\cdot 10^{-5}\) \(3{,}95\cdot 10^{-4}\) \(0{,}10\)
\(0{,}5\) \(3{,}1\cdot 10^{-2}\) \(2{,}47\cdot 10^{-4}\) \(9{,}87\cdot 10^{-4}\) \(0{,}25\)
\(1\) \(6{,}3\cdot 10^{-2}\) \(9{,}87\cdot 10^{-4}\) \(1{,}97\cdot 10^{-3}\) \(0{,}50\)

The table says that at \(w_0 = h/5\) the stretch of the middle plane (\(3{,}95\cdot 10^{-5}\)) counts for \(10\) % of the bending strain (\(3{,}95\cdot 10^{-4}\)). That is the limit we took in idealization 2: at it we neglect ten percent of the strain. At \(w_0 = h\) the stretch would already be half of the bending strain and the model would be wrong. How wrong, we do not compute here. Large deflections are described by the theory of von Kármán, which the book does not treat: VK (PDF p. 11) says that the final form of the equation of large deflections was developed by von Kármán. The slope at \(w_0 = h/5\) is still well below the limit: \(w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 1{,}6\cdot 10^{-4} \le 10^{-2}\).

Theorem 18.3 gives us all the strains from one function. The function that records how the plate curves, we name.

Definition 18.4 Curvatures of a plate (ukrivljenosti plošče)

Let \(w\) be the deflection of a Kirchhoff plate, a twice continuously differentiable function on \(\Omega\) (theorem 18.3). The curvatures of a plate are the functions of the point \((x, y)\)

\[\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{xx}} , \qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = w_{\mathrm{yy}} , \qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{xy}} = w_{\mathrm{xy}} , \tag{18.4}\]

each with the unit \(\mathrm{m}^{-1}\), each giving one number at every point. \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the curvature of the curve \(w(\cdot, y)\) in the section plane \(y = \text{constant}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}\) of the curve \(w(x, \cdot)\), and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the twist (zvitje): the rate of change of the slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) in the direction \(y\).

Source: EP (7.2.79) (p. 428) has the derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) in the strains, VK (2.7) (PDF p. 24) has curvatures with the opposite sign, because VK counts \(w\) downwards. Our \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\) is as for the beam in definition 5.16, \(\kappa = v''\).

We see the curvature in the direction \(x\) in figure 18.2: the curve is a section of the middle plane, its second derivative is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\). The curvature in the direction \(y\) is the same picture in the section \(x = \text{constant}\). The twist \(\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is new, the beam has none, and so it has its own moment, as we shall see. With \(\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}} \ne 0\) the plate twists like a piece of cardboard pulled up at two diagonal corners and down at the other two (section 18.2). For a small slope (\(w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 \le 10^{-2}\)) \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\) is an approximation of the exact curvature \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}/(1 + w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)^{3/2}\), which differs from it by less than \(1{,}5\) % (relatively \(\tfrac32 w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 \le 1{,}5\cdot 10^{-2}\)), as for the beam (definition 5.16).

18.1.3 Moments and stresses

Now we compute the stresses from the strains and from them the forces in the cross-section. For the beam the cross-section is a segment or a rectangle and the forces in it are three numbers: the axial force, the shear force and the moment (lemma 5.9). For the plate the section with the plane \(x = \text{constant}\) is a rectangle of height \(h\) and arbitrary width, and we measure the forces along it per unit length. In figure 18.3 let us see which parts of the stress give the moments.

Each panel shows a piece of plate (panel (c) its face), with the thickness enlarged for the drawing, and its middle plane, drawn dashed. Panel (a) shows the section of the plate with the plane \(y = \text{constant}\), with the axis \(x\) to the right and \(z\) up, and a piece cut at \(x\) and \(x + 3\) (drawing units). On each of the two faces of the piece acts the longitudinal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\): above it presses on the face, below it pulls, and the arrows are longer the farther from the middle plane they lie. The sum of these forces over the height is zero, because the stress is an odd function of \(z\), and what remains is a pair of forces, that is a moment. We denote it \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\). In panel (b) is the same conclusion in the section \(x = \text{constant}\), with the axis \(y\) to the right, with the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and the moment \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\). In panel (c) we look at the face \(x = \text{constant}\) from the front, with the axis \(y\) to the right and \(z\) up: the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is directed one way above and the opposite way below, and their pair is the twisting moment \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The shear stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) give the transverse forces, which we introduce in the next section.

Definition 18.5 Moments of a plate (momenti plošče)

Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) be continuous functions of the variables \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) on a plate of thickness \(h\) (definition 18.1). The bending moments (upogibna momenta) \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) and the twisting moment (zvojni moment) \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) of the plate are functions of the point \((x, y)\) of the middle plane

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad M_{\mathrm{y}} = -\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\mathrm{d}z , \quad M_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}z . \tag{18.5}\]

They have the unit N m/m: a moment per unit length of the edge, since the integral is over the height and not over the width. A positive \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) means compression above the middle plane and tension below it, like the positive moment of the beam \(M = -\int y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) (lemma 5.9). The longitudinal forces per unit length of the edge are \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}z\) and \(N_{\mathrm{y}} = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\mathrm{d}z\), the in-plane shear force \(N_{\mathrm{xy}} = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}z\).

Source: EP (7.2.83) (p. 429) has \(M_{\mathrm{xx}} = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,z\,\mathrm{d}z\) without the minus, so its sign is opposite to ours. VK (2.12) (PDF p. 26) has \(z\) downwards and a positive moment for tensile stresses in the lower half of the plate, which is the same physical sign as ours (compression above, tension below). The moment of the beam \(M = -\int y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) (lemma 5.9) has the same sign.

Let us say specifically why we took the minus. For the beam we took \(M = -\int y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) so that \(M = EI\,v''\) has no minus (theorem 5.35). We shall get the same for the plate: \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) when \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). The naming: bending, because \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) bend the plate, twisting, because \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) twists the plate, as we shall see in the example. The index of \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the index of the stress from which the moment comes, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), not the axis about which the moment turns. The moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) turns about the axis \(y\).

Before we compute the moments, we need a quantity that says how much moment belongs to a curvature, like \(EI\) for the beam.

Definition 18.6 Flexural rigidity of a plate (upogibna togost plošče)

Let a plate of thickness \(h\) be made of a homogeneous isotropic material with modulus of elasticity \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\), \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\). The flexural rigidity of a plate is the number

\[D = \frac{E\,h^3}{12\,(1 - \nu^2)} , \tag{18.6}\]

with the unit N m.

Source: VK (2.14) (PDF p. 27), EP (7.2.89) (p. 430), ONATE2 (5.15) (PDF p. 270). For the beam the corresponding quantity is \(EI\) of definition 5.36, and for a beam of unit width \(I = h^3/12\).

Let us explain each term. The factor \(h^3/12\) is the integral \(\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} z^2\,\mathrm{d}z\) (theorem 3.40, \(\big[z^3/3\big]_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} = h^3/12\)), the second moment of area of a cross-section \(1\) wide and \(h\) high about the middle plane. \(E/(1 - \nu^2)\) is the modulus of a layer in plane stress when the layer cannot contract sideways (theorem 18.7 below). For our example \(D = 196\cdot 10^9\cdot 10^{-6}/(12\cdot 0{,}91) = 17\,948{,}7\) N m, while the rigidity of a beam of unit width is \(EI = E h^3/12 = 16\,333{,}3\) N m. The ratio is \(D/EI = 1/(1 - \nu^2) = 1{,}0989\).

Theorem 18.7 Moments of a plate from curvatures (momenti plošče iz ukrivljenosti)

Let the plate be a Kirchhoff plate (definition 18.2), with strains by theorem 18.3. Then the stresses in the layer \(z\) are

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\frac{E\,z}{1 - \nu^2}\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\frac{E\,z}{1 - \nu^2}\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\frac{E\,z}{1 + \nu}\,\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}} , \tag{18.7}\]

the longitudinal forces \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = N_{\mathrm{y}} = N_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) and the moments

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}) , \qquad M_{\mathrm{y}} = D\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}) , \qquad M_{\mathrm{xy}} = D\,(1 - \nu)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}} . \tag{18.8}\]
Proof

We must show the stresses of a layer from Hooke's law, then the integrals over the thickness. We use idealization 5, that is a layer in plane stress with \(E' = E\) and \(\nu' = \nu\).

  1. By equation (11.43) with \(E' = E\) and \(\nu' = \nu\) we have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}})/E\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = (1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/E\).
  2. We invert. To the first equation we add \(\nu\) times the second: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \big( \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} - \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \nu^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} \big)/E = (1 - \nu^2)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\). Hence \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})/(1 - \nu^2)\) and, swapping \(x \leftrightarrow y\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})/(1 - \nu^2)\). The third equation gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}/(1 + \nu)\).
  3. We insert the strains of equation (18.3), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -z\,\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -z\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -z\,\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}\). These are the stresses (18.7).
  4. All three stresses are linear in \(z\), so odd functions of \(z\) at constant \(x\), \(y\). The integral of an odd function over \([-h/2, h/2]\) is zero, hence \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = N_{\mathrm{y}} = N_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\).
  5. For the moments we take out the coefficients that do not depend on \(z\) (lemma 3.39) and use \(\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} z^2\,\mathrm{d}z = h^3/12\): \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}z = \dfrac{E\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}})}{1 - \nu^2}\cdot\dfrac{h^3}{12} = D\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}})\). Likewise \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  6. For the twisting moment, \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = \dfrac{E\,\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}}{1 + \nu}\cdot\dfrac{h^3}{12}\). Since \(\dfrac{E}{1 + \nu} = \dfrac{E\,(1 - \nu)}{1 - \nu^2}\), this is \(D\,(1 - \nu)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

Source: VK (2.10), (2.13) (PDF pp. 26-27), EP (7.2.87)-(7.2.89) (p. 430), ONATE2 (5.13)-(5.15) (PDF p. 270). We compared the signs at definition 18.5 and checked the relations with SymPy.

The theorem says two things. First, the moments \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) are coupled: \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) depends not only on \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\) but also on \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}\) through \(\nu\). The transverse curvature therefore changes the moment in the direction \(x\). Second, the twisting moment \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is proportional to the twist. For the beam \(M = EI\,v''\), this is theorem 5.35. For the plate the same theorem splits into three.

Corollary 18.8 Stresses of a plate from moments (napetosti plošče iz momentov)

Let theorem 18.7 hold. Then

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\frac{12\,M_{\mathrm{x}}}{h^3}\,z , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\frac{12\,M_{\mathrm{y}}}{h^3}\,z , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\frac{12\,M_{\mathrm{xy}}}{h^3}\,z , \tag{18.9}\]

and the largest absolute value of each of them at a point of the middle plane, along its normal, is on the faces \(z = \pm h/2\):

\[|\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}|_{\max} = \frac{6\,|M_{\mathrm{x}}|}{h^2} , \qquad |\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}|_{\max} = \frac{6\,|M_{\mathrm{y}}|}{h^2} , \qquad |\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}|_{\max} = \frac{6\,|M_{\mathrm{xy}}|}{h^2} . \tag{18.10}\]
Proof

We must show that \(E/(1 - \nu^2)\) and \(E/(1 + \nu)\) are expressed by \(D\) and that \(|z| \le h/2\).

  1. From \(D = E h^3/(12\,(1 - \nu^2))\) we have \(E/(1 - \nu^2) = 12\,D/h^3\). The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of theorem 18.7 is therefore \(-12\,D\,z\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}})/h^3 = -12\,M_{\mathrm{x}}\,z/h^3\), because \(D\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}) = M_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\).
  2. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(E/(1 + \nu) = 12\,D\,(1 - \nu)/h^3\), and \(-12\,D\,(1 - \nu)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}\,z/h^3 = -12\,M_{\mathrm{xy}}\,z/h^3\).
  3. The absolute value \(|z| \le h/2\) is largest at \(|z| = h/2\), where \(12\,|M|\,(h/2)/h^3 = 6\,|M|/h^2\).

Source: Stresses from moments: VK (2.15) (PDF p. 27). The largest stress \(6\,M/h^2\) is the same as for the beam at \(\sigma = M\,h/(2I) = 6\,M/h^2\) for \(I = h^3/12\).

Let us test the corollary on the example. Take our plate, curved only in the direction \(x\) with \(w = -x^2/(2R)\), \(R = 50\) m, so \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}02\) 1/m, \(w_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) (in the direction \(y\) it is held by the neighbouring parts, which section 18.4 will show in more detail). At \(x = 0{,}25\) m the deflection is \(0{,}625\) mm, that is \(0{,}06\,h\). The strain on the upper face (\(z = h/2 = 5\) mm) is by equation (18.3) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1{,}00\cdot 10^{-4}\), tension. The stress by theorem 18.7 is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}/(1 - \nu^2) = 21{,}538\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 6{,}462\) MPa, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). The moment is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -358{,}97\) N m/m and \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = \nu\,M_{\mathrm{x}} = -107{,}69\) N m/m. By the corollary 18.8, \(6\,|M_{\mathrm{x}}|/h^2 = 6\cdot 358{,}97/10^{-4} = 21{,}538\) MPa and \(6\,|M_{\mathrm{y}}|/h^2 = 6{,}462\) MPa, all three calculations agree. The moment is negative because the upper face is in tension: by definition 18.5 the moment is positive for compression above, and here it is just the opposite.

Now the twist: the plate \(w = c\,x\,y\) with \(c = 0{,}01\) 1/m has \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = w_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xy}} = c\). By theorem 18.7 \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = M_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = (1 - \nu)\,D\,c = 125{,}64\) N m/m, so by the corollary \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}|_{\max} = 6\,M_{\mathrm{xy}}/h^2 = 7{,}538\) MPa and the shear strain is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1{,}00\cdot 10^{-4}\) on the face. A plate that has no bending curvature in the direction of the axes thus has a twisting moment. We check correctness in rotated axes: the surface \(x\,y = (s^2 - t^2)/2\) in axes \(s\), \(t\) rotated by \(45^\circ\) has curvatures \(c\) and \(-c\) (SymPy), and the bending moment from the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ss}}\) is, by theorem 18.7 written in these axes, \(D\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{s}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{t}}) = D\,(1 - \nu)\,c = M_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The twist is thus only bending in oblique directions.

18.1.4 Test: a narrow beam is not a plate

Theorem 18.7 holds for every Kirchhoff plate, but \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} + \nu\,\kappa_{\mathrm{y}})\) differs from \(EI\,\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\), which the beam has. Let us see when each relation gives the right moment. Take the same steel part, bent with the same curvature \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}02\) 1/m, but in two cases (figure 18.4).

In panel (a) the body is a narrow beam of width \(b = 10\) mm, of a similar size as \(h\). Its sides are free. Nothing prevents the sideways deformation, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) in every layer and the upper, stretched layers contract sideways by Poisson's effect by \(-\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), while the lower, compressed layers expand. The section of the beam therefore curves the other way, a phenomenon called anticlastic curvature (antiklastična ukrivljenost, from Greek anti, opposite, and klasis, break: curvature of the opposite sign). In panel (b) is a piece of a wide plate, where the neighbouring parts hold the sides and a layer cannot contract sideways: \(w_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \nu\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), as in the example above. The same body behaves differently depending on whether it is free or held at the side.

The calculation for the narrow beam. Theorem 18.7 does not hold here: a narrow beam is not a thin plate, since idealization 1 requires \(h/a \le 0{,}05\), while here the width \(b\) equals the thickness \(h\). The narrow beam is the beam of chapter 5 with fibres in uniaxial stress, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) in every layer. The fibre at height \(z\) has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and contracts sideways by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \nu\,z\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (definition 3.2). A sideways strain linear in \(z\) means a transverse curvature: as for the plate in equation (18.3), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{yy}}\), so \(w_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = +0{,}006\) 1/m, a radius of curvature of \(166{,}67\) m (SymPy). Across the width \(b = 10\) mm the edge rises relative to the centre by \(\tfrac12\,w_{\mathrm{yy}}\,(b/2)^2 = 0{,}075\ \mu\mathrm{m}\), which is very little and is therefore enlarged in the figure. The moment is given by theorem 5.35, \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) with \(I = b\,h^3/12\). For the whole beam of width \(b = 10\) mm, \(M = -3{,}267\) N m, and per unit width \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = \dfrac{E h^3}{12}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -326{,}67\) N m/m, which is \(D\,(1 - \nu^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The stress on the upper face is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -E\,\tfrac h2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 19{,}600\) MPa, while \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is zero, as the free sides require.

In a plate curved only in the direction \(x\) (\(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), panel (b)) we have \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -358{,}97\) N m/m and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 21{,}538\) MPa. The ratio of the stresses of the beam and the plate is \(19{,}600/21{,}538 = 0{,}9100 = 1 - \nu^2\). If we computed the narrow beam with the plate formula, we would overestimate the moment and stress by \(1/0{,}91 - 1 = 9{,}9\) %, and if we computed the plate as a beam, we would underestimate them by \(9\) %. This is the test: a plate is not a beam, \(D\) is not \(EI\), and which relation holds is decided by whether the neighbouring parts hold the lateral sides. Where the limit between the two cases lies, we do not compute. For a plate curved only in the direction \(x\), section 18.4 computes the deflection and the moment and compares them with the beam.

18.1.5 What the Kirchhoff model neglects

For the beam, section 5.3.4 listed what the model neglects. Here we do the same for the plate and estimate with numbers how much.

Shear stress. The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero, but the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are not, since they carry the transverse forces. In the next section we compute them from equilibrium and it turns out that they run across the thickness as a parabola, largest at \(z = 0\) and zero on the faces, as for the beam (theorem 5.39). The mean of the function \(1 - 4z^2/h^2\) across the thickness is \(\tfrac1h\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}(1 - 4z^2/h^2)\,\mathrm{d}z = \tfrac23\) (SymPy), its largest value \(1\) is therefore one and a half times the mean, and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) at \(z = 0\) is one and a half times the mean stress \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}/h\).

Transverse normal stress. Idealization 5 sets \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), but by idealization 3 \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), whereas Hooke's law at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}})/E\). For the plate of the example above, on the upper face \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,(1 + \nu)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E = -4{,}29\cdot 10^{-5}\). That is \(43\) % of the bending strain \(1{,}00\cdot 10^{-4}\), but it acts only across the thickness: the change of the half-thickness \(h/2 = 5\) mm is on average \(-2{,}14\cdot 10^{-5}\) times \(5\) mm, that is \(-0{,}107\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). That is \(2{,}1\cdot 10^{-5}\) of the half-thickness and \(1{,}7\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the deflection \(0{,}625\) mm. We therefore neglect a strain that is large compared with the bending strain, but it affects the shape of the plate only by a tenth of a micrometre.

Limit of thickness. Idealization 1 is \(h/a \le 0{,}05\). Our plate has \(0{,}02\), so \(a/h = 50\). By ONATE2 (PDF p. 268) the condition of a perpendicular normal holds only up to \(h/a = 0{,}05\). In moderately thick (\(0{,}05 \le h/a < 0{,}10\)) and very thick plates (\(h/a \ge 0{,}10\)) the normal distorts more and more during deformation, and a better approximation is a theory with an independent rotation of the normal (section 18.8). For \(a/h = 5\), \(10\), \(20\) we shall compute later by how much the deflection differs from the Kirchhoff one.

18.1.6 Notation in this chapter

The plate uses letters that the book already has for other quantities. Let us list them so that we do not make a mistake.

  • \(w\) is the deflection of the plate, as for the vibration of the beam in chapter 13. For the static beam (chapter 5) the deflection was \(v\), the same quantity.
  • \(h\) is the thickness of the plate. In chapter 12 \(h\) is the length of an element, so in plate elements we write \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\). In chapter 14 \(h\) is the heat transfer coefficient, and we never use the two together.
  • \(D\) is the flexural rigidity of the plate in N m. In chapter 4 \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a compliance, always with two indices.
  • \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are moments per unit length in N m/m, for the beam \(M\) is a moment in N m. The sign is as for the beam: at \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and for the beam \(M = EI\,v''\) (equation (5.24)), both positive for compression above.
  • \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) are transverse forces per unit length in N/m (section 18.2). For the beam the shear force is \(V\) in N, in chapter 14 \(Q\) is a heat source.
  • \(q\) is the load per unit area in N/m\(^2\), for the beam per unit length in N/m.
  • \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are the curvatures of the plate, for the beam \(\kappa = v''\).
  • \(\theta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{y}}\) will be the rotations of the normals in the Mindlin plate (section 18.8), \(\theta\) is the rotation of the cross-section in the Timoshenko beam. \(k\) is the shear correction factor as for the beam (definition 5.86), in chapter 14 it is conductivity. \(N_{\mathrm{x}}\) is a longitudinal force per unit length in N/m, for the beam the axial force \(N\) in N.

The sign: the axis \(z\) points up, and \(w\) and the load \(q\) are positive in the same direction. This choice keeps the right-handed triple of axes and the sign of the moment as for the beam (\(M > 0\) for compression above). If the load presses downwards, \(q < 0\). Since the results of the chapter are linear in \(q\), every result then has the sign opposite to that for a load of the same size upwards.

In the next section we introduce the transverse forces and the load and from the equilibrium of a piece of plate derive the equation that determines the deflection (section 18.2).

18.2 Equilibrium of a plate

In the previous section we described the plate by the deflection \(w(x, y)\) of its middle plane and computed from it the displacements, strains, stresses and the moments \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) per unit length. The deflection itself is not yet known. For a beam we get it from the deflection curve equation \(EI\,v'''' = q\) (theorem 5.42), which follows from the equilibrium of a piece of the beam (lemma 5.10). This section takes the same road in two dimensions. We ask three questions. Which forces besides the moments must a piece of plate carry to be in equilibrium? Which equation connects the deflection \(w\) with the load \(q\)? And which stress belongs to these forces, when the Kirchhoff model cannot compute them from the strain, which in it is zero (section 5.3.4)?

Take the plate as fixed in section 18.1: homogeneous, isotropic, linearly elastic, of constant thickness \(h\), with modulus of elasticity \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\), and with rigidity \(D = E h^3/(12(1 - \nu^2))\) (definition 18.6). The middle plane is the plane \(xy\) and the axis \(z\) is perpendicular to it and points the same way as the deflection \(w\) and the load \(q\), as in equation (13.31) for the beam. Our example is a steel plate with \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(h = 10\) mm. Then \(D = 17\,948{,}7\) N m and the shear modulus is \(G = 75{,}385\) GPa. The load is \(q = 10\) kPa, that is \(10\,000\) N in the direction \(z\) on every square metre of the middle plane.

18.2.1 Transverse shear forces

Cut a piece out of the plate: a rectangle \(R = [x_1, x_2] \times [y_1, y_2]\) of the middle plane together with the material above and below it up to both surfaces of the plate (piece, figure 18.5). We drew the thickness much larger than the true one, and the dashed plane is the middle plane. We put the coordinates beside the piece as axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), with \(z\) pointing up, as in section 18.1, and the load \(q\) positive in the direction \(z\).

Three influences act on the piece. The first is the load \(q\), a force \(q\) per unit area, acting on the upper surface. It is drawn for \(q > 0\), so upward. A downward load, such as weight, has \(q < 0\) (section 18.1). Because of it the total force on the piece is \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} q\,\mathrm{d}A\) and it points in the direction \(z\). The second and third come through the side faces, where the rest of the plate is cut away: there the stress vector acts on the piece (definition 2.20). By Newton the equilibrium of the piece demands that the sum of all forces on it is zero (definition 2.3). At least one of these forces must therefore oppose the load in the direction \(z\).

Which one? Look at the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the right face. It is drawn as a pair of forces: at the top the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) pushes the face inward, at the bottom it pulls it outward, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is linear through the thickness and changes sign at \(z = 0\) (theorem 18.3). Both forces are horizontal, their sum in the direction \(z\) is zero, and so the pair cannot carry the load. The same holds for the pair \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) on the front face and for the pairs \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which the shear stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) in the plane of the plate give. By Cauchy's formula the component \(z\) of the stress vector on a face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), and on a face with normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) it is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) (equation (2.24)). The vertical force through the side faces is therefore carried by the shear stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) alone. This is the same conclusion as for the beam: there the transverse force \(V\) came from the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (lemma 5.9). For the plate we write it per unit length of the edge, like the moments.

Definition 18.9 Transverse shear forces of a plate (prečni sili plošče)

Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) be continuous functions on a plate of thickness \(h\) whose middle plane lies in the plane \(xy\). The transverse shear forces of the plate are the functions of the point \((x, y)\) of the middle plane

\[Q_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y) = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \qquad Q_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y) = \int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2} \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z . \tag{18.11}\]

Their unit is N/m, force per unit length of edge. \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the \(z\) component of the force per unit length with which the part of the plate at larger \(x\) acts on the part at smaller \(x\), and similarly \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\). The load \(q\) is the force per unit area of the middle plane in the direction \(z\) and includes the weight of the plate.

Source: EP (7.2.100) (p. 433) and ONATE2 (PDF p. 272-273) write \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) for the same shear forces, VK (PDF p. 29) too. The sign with respect to the normal of the face is ours, as in lemma 5.9.

In the figure we see them as \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the right face and \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) on the front face. On the name: the force is transverse because it acts across the middle plane, perpendicular to it, in contrast to the forces in the plane of the plate. The letter \(Q\) comes from the sources. In chapter 5 the transverse force of a beam was \(V\) in N, here \(Q\) is in N/m, and in chapter 14 \(Q\) is a heat source, but we shall never mix the two chapters. Also \(q\) is now a force per unit area, not per unit length. All forces in the plane of the middle plane, for instance \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}z\), are zero in pure bending, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is an odd function of \(z\) and the integral of an odd function over \([-h/2, h/2]\) is zero. So the load passes through the piece by \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) alone.

For the moments we keep the sign of the previous section, which follows chapter 5 (\(M = -\int y\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) for a beam): \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}z\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = -\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\mathrm{d}z\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}z\), all integrals over \([-h/2, h/2]\) (definition 18.5). By theorem 18.7 \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D(w_{\mathrm{xx}} + \nu\,w_{\mathrm{yy}})\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = D(w_{\mathrm{yy}} + \nu\,w_{\mathrm{xx}})\) and \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = D(1 - \nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

18.2.2 Equilibrium of a piece of plate

Now we can write the equilibrium of the piece. The piece transmits forces and moments only through its side faces. We write them with the stress vector, which Cauchy's formula gives from the stresses (theorem 2.24). On the right face the outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), on the left \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), on the back side face \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), on the front \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). Let \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\) be the outward normal of the boundary \(\partial R\) of the rectangle in the plane \(xy\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{n}} = Q_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\). We write \(\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} f\,\mathrm{d}s\) for the sum of the integrals over the four sides of the rectangle.

Lemma 18.10 Equilibrium of a piece of a plate (ravnovesje kosa plošče)

Let the plate be as above and in equilibrium, and let all stress components be continuous. On one surface let a force \(q(x, y)\) per unit area act in the direction \(z\) with a continuous function \(q\), let the other surface be free, and let body forces be included in \(q\). Let \(R = [x_1, x_2] \times [y_1, y_2]\) be a rectangle in the middle plane that does not reach beyond the edge of the plate. Then

\[\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_{\mathrm{R}} q\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \tag{18.12}\]
\[\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} \big( y\,Q_{\mathrm{n}} + M_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_{\mathrm{R}} y\,q\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \tag{18.13}\]
\[\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} \big( x\,Q_{\mathrm{n}} + M_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_{\mathrm{R}} x\,q\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 . \tag{18.14}\]
Proof

We must show three equalities: the equilibrium of forces in the direction \(z\) and the equilibrium of moments about the axis \(x\) and the axis \(y\) through the origin. The moment of every force is computed as \(\vek r\times\vek t\) and integrated through the thickness.

  1. The piece \(P = R \times [-h/2, h/2]\) is a body made of boxes and it is in equilibrium, so the sum of the forces on it is zero and the sum of the moments about the origin is zero (definition 2.3, equations (2.2) and (2.35)). The forces on it are: the forces through the four side faces, the force of the load on one surface and nothing through the free surface. The force through a face is the integral of the stress vector \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) (theorem 2.24, equation (2.24)), with \(t_{\mathrm{z}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\), since \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\).
  2. The side face \(x = x_2\) is the rectangle \([y_1, y_2] \times [-h/2, h/2]\) with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). The integral over it is by the definition of the integral over a rectangle an iterated integral, first over \(z\) and then over \(y\). The inner integral of the component \(t_{\mathrm{z}}\) is \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}z = Q_{\mathrm{x}}(x_2, y)\) (definition 18.9). Over \(y\) we integrate \(Q_{\mathrm{n}} = Q_{\mathrm{x}}\). The same holds on the face \(x = x_1\) with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\), and on the faces \(y = y_2\), \(y = y_1\) with \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\). The sum of the \(z\) components of the forces through the side faces is therefore \(\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  3. The force of the load in the direction \(z\) is \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} q\,\mathrm{d}A\). The equilibrium of forces in the direction \(z\) is therefore equation (18.12).
  4. The moment about the origin of the forces through a face is the integral \(\int \vek r\times\vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\) with \(\vek r = (x, y, z)\) (definition of the moment of a force, as in lemma 11.2). The component \(x\) of \(\vek r\times\vek t\) is \(y\,t_{\mathrm{z}} - z\,t_{\mathrm{y}}\) and the component \(y\) is \(z\,t_{\mathrm{x}} - x\,t_{\mathrm{z}}\) (equation (2.32)). On a side face with normal \((n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) we have \(t_{\mathrm{y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\). On this face \(x\) and \(y\) are constant when we integrate over \(z\). So the integral of the component \(x\) through the thickness is \(y\,Q_{\mathrm{n}} - n_{\mathrm{x}}\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\mathrm{d}z - n_{\mathrm{y}}\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\mathrm{d}z = y\,Q_{\mathrm{n}} + M_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\), where we used the definitions of the moments and the symmetry of stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (theorem 2.36). In the same way the integral of the component \(y\) through the thickness is \(-\big(x\,Q_{\mathrm{n}} + M_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\big)\).
  5. The load is a distributed force with density \(q\) in the direction \(z\). Its moment is \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} \vek r\times(0, 0, q)\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{R}} (y\,q, -x\,q, 0)\,\mathrm{d}A\), whichever surface it acts on, since the height \(z\) of the point of application does not enter the components \(x\) and \(y\). The equilibrium of the component \(x\) of the moments is therefore equation (18.13), and that of the component \(y\) is (18.14) after multiplication by \(-1\).
  6. The other three balances (forces in the directions \(x\) and \(y\), moment about the axis \(z\)) are not needed here. The forces in the plane are zero because \(N_{\mathrm{x}} = N_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and the normal stresses are odd in \(z\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The sources derive the same three equations with a small element of the plate: VK (2.19)-(2.21) (PDF p. 29), ONATE2 (5.21)-(5.23) (PDF p. 272-273), EP with Hamilton's principle (7.2.98) (p. 433). Our way does not use a small element but a finite piece, as for the beam (lemma 5.10).

Let us test the lemma on a field that is a simple polynomial, \(w = q\,(x^4 + y^4)/(48\,D)\). It is not the solution of any supported plate, but it is a field with known moments. By theorem 18.7 \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = (q/4)(x^2 + \nu\,y^2)\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = (q/4)(y^2 + \nu\,x^2)\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). We take the transverse forces from the moment balances, as the theorem below will get them in a point: \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -q\,x/2\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{y}} = -q\,y/2\) (SymPy). So the test does not check the moment balances, which hold by construction, but the balance of forces, which the true \(w\) satisfies only because of the plate equation. Take the piece \([0{,}1,\ 0{,}3] \times [0{,}2,\ 0{,}4]\) m at \(q = 10\) kPa. Its area is \(0{,}04\) m², the force of the load is \(400\) N. Over the sides \(\int Q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) is \(-300\) N on the right (\(x = 0{,}3\)), \(+100\) N on the left (\(x = 0{,}1\)), \(-400\) N on the back (\(y = 0{,}4\)) and \(+200\) N on the front (\(y = 0{,}2\)), together \(-400\) N, and equation (18.12) holds: \(-400 + 400 = 0\). The moment (18.13) has \(-120\) N m on the boundary and \(+120\) N m from the load, the moment (18.14) has \(-80\) N m on the boundary and \(+80\) N m from the load, both in balance.

What if we left out the transverse forces, as if the model did not need them? The moments on the boundary alone would give \(+60\) N m and \(+40\) N m, while the moments of the load are \(120\) N m and \(80\) N m. The sums would be \(60 + 120 = 180\) N m and \(40 + 80 = 120\) N m instead of zero. So the moment pairs alone do not balance the piece. The balance holds only with the transverse forces, which contribute \(-180\) N m and \(-120\) N m on the boundary (SymPy).

18.2.3 The plate equation

Equations (18.12), (18.13) and (18.14) hold for every rectangle. From them we want equations at a point. For the beam we shrank the piece and got a derivative. For the plate we take a rectangle and turn the boundary integrals into integrals over the piece: this is the divergence theorem in the plane, which we prove for a rectangle right here, with the same steps as point 1 of theorem 4.14. Then we use that a function whose integral over every rectangle is zero is zero (as in lemma 4.83).

Lemma 18.11 Divergence theorem in the plane for a rectangle (izrek o divergenci v ravnini za pravokotnik)

Let \(U\) be an open set in the plane \(xy\).

  1. Let \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}})\) be a continuously differentiable field on \(U\) (definition 1.90). For every rectangle \(R = [x_1, x_2] \times [y_1, y_2] \subseteq U\) with outward normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}})\) on \(\partial R\)
    \[\int_{\mathrm{R}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} \big( v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{18.15}\]
  2. If \(f\) is continuous on \(U\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) for every rectangle \(R \subseteq U\) with sides parallel to the axes, then \(f = 0\) at every point of \(U\).
Proof

We must show both points. The first is point 1 of theorem 4.14 in the plane, the second is a conclusion by shrinking a rectangle around a point.

  1. The function \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\) is continuous on \(R\). By the theorem on the order of integration (theorem 4.9) \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} \partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{y}_1}^{y_2}\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} \partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\), and by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, point 1) the inner integral is \(v_{\mathrm{x}}(x_2, y) - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x_1, y)\). On the side \(x = x_2\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), on the side \(x = x_1\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\) and on the horizontal sides \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so this is \(\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. For \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) we exchange the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) and get \(\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}s\). The sum of both equalities is (18.15).
  3. Let \(f(P) \ne 0\) at some point \(P \in U\), without loss of generality \(f(P) > 0\). By continuity there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that the square \(R\) of half-side \(\delta\) around \(P\) lies in \(U\) and \(f \ge f(P)/2\) on \(R\). By monotonicity and the constant function (lemma 4.10, points 4 and 2, for a rectangle) \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} f\,\mathrm{d}A \ge f(P)/2 \cdot 4\delta^2 > 0\), which contradicts the assumption. Hence \(f(P) = 0\).

Source: Point 1 follows the proof of point 1 of theorem 4.14 for a box with the variable \(z\) removed. Point 2 is the plane form of lemma 4.83, without weights, because the function is continuous. The proof is not from the sources.

The story of this equation begins far from mechanics.

From history

Chladni covered a plate with fine sand and showed the nodal lines of its various modes of vibration, and with them he also determined the corresponding frequencies (TIMO PDF p. 127). In 1809 the French Academy invited him to demonstrate his experiments, Napoleon attended, and at the emperor's suggestion the Academy proposed as the subject of a prize essay a mathematical theory of the vibration of plates, compared with experiment (TIMO PDF p. 127). In October 1811, at the closing date of the competition, only one candidate appeared, Sophie Germain (TIMO PDF p. 128). She knew Euler's work on elastic curves, where the equation of the deflection is derived from the energy of bending with the calculus of variations, and she decided to proceed in the same way: she assumed that the strain energy of a plate is the integral of an expression with the principal radii of curvature \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) of the surface (TIMO PDF p. 128). She made a mistake in calculating the variation, did not find the correct equation and did not win the prize. Lagrange, one of the judges, noticed the error and after corrections obtained the required equation (TIMO PDF p. 128, VK PDF p. 30). The Academy proposed the subject again with a new closing date in October 1813. Germain now had the correct equation, but the judges required a physical justification of her assumption about the energy. She again did not succeed, and she won the prize only the third time, in 1816, although the judges were not quite satisfied with her work (TIMO PDF p. 128). Poisson showed that the equation follows not only from Germain's integral but also from another integral, which with a proper choice of constants is the correct expression for the strain energy of bending. This explained why Germain found the correct equation, although her quantity is not the strain energy of a bent plate (TIMO PDF p. 129).

So the equation was found from an energy that was not the right one, and yet the equation was right. How this is possible we shall test on an example, but first we derive the equation from the equilibrium of a piece, which needs no energy.

Theorem 18.12 Plate equation (enačba plošče)

Let the plate be as in lemma 18.10, with constant \(E\) and \(h\). Let \(w\) be four times continuously differentiable on the middle plane, let \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) be as in theorem 18.7, and let \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) be continuously differentiable. Then

\[Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -D\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\nabla^2 w , \qquad Q_{\mathrm{y}} = -D\,\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\nabla^2 w , \tag{18.16}\]

and

\[D\,\nabla^4 w = q , \qquad \nabla^4 w = \frac{\partial^4 w}{\partial x^4} + 2\,\frac{\partial^4 w}{\partial x^2\,\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^4 w}{\partial y^4} . \tag{18.17}\]
Proof

We must show that the equilibrium of every rectangle gives three equations at a point, and that these give equation (18.17). Every rectangle in the middle plane is a piece as in lemma 18.10. We use the divergence theorem in the plane (lemma 18.11) and the vanishing integrand.

  1. The field \(\vek v = (Q_{\mathrm{x}}, Q_{\mathrm{y}})\) is continuously differentiable, so by lemma 18.11, point 1, \(\int_{\partial \mathrm{R}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_{\mathrm{R}} (Q_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A\). Equation (18.12) gives \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} (Q_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}} + q)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) for every rectangle. By point 2 of the lemma
    \[Q_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}} + q = 0 . \tag{18.18}\]
  2. The field \(\vek v = (y\,Q_{\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy}},\ y\,Q_{\mathrm{y}} + M_{\mathrm{y}})\) is continuously differentiable (the differentiability of \(M\) follows from \(w\) being four times continuously differentiable). Its divergence is \(Q_{\mathrm{y}} + y\,(Q_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}}) + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}}\), since \(\partial y/\partial y = 1\). Equation (18.13) by the lemma, point 1, and by step 1 gives \(\int_{\mathrm{R}} \big( Q_{\mathrm{y}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{R}} y\,(Q_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}} + q)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\). The second integral is zero by equation (18.18). By point 2 of the lemma \(Q_{\mathrm{y}} = -(M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}})\).
  3. The field \((x\,Q_{\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{x}},\ x\,Q_{\mathrm{y}} + M_{\mathrm{xy}})\) has the divergence \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} + x\,(Q_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + Q_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}}) + M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}}\). The same conclusion with equation (18.14) gives \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -(M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}})\).
  4. We insert the moments of theorem 18.7, \(D\) is constant: \(M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}} = D\,(w_{\mathrm{xxx}} + \nu\,w_{\mathrm{yyx}} + (1 - \nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xyy}}) = D\,(w_{\mathrm{xxx}} + w_{\mathrm{xyy}})\), since mixed derivatives are equal (theorem 8.30). This is \(D\,\partial\nabla^2 w/\partial x\). Similarly \(M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}} = D\,\partial\nabla^2 w/\partial y\). Equations (18.16) are proved.
  5. We insert into (18.18): \(-D\,(\nabla^2 w)_{\mathrm{xx}} - D\,(\nabla^2 w)_{\mathrm{yy}} + q = 0\), and \((\nabla^2 w)_{\mathrm{xx}} + (\nabla^2 w)_{\mathrm{yy}} = w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + 2\,w_{\mathrm{xxyy}} + w_{\mathrm{yyyy}}\). This is (18.17).

Source: EP (7.2.98) (p. 433) with \(M_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) of the opposite sign, because EP writes \(M_{\mathrm{xx}} = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,z\,\mathrm{d}z\) (7.2.83), VK (2.19)-(2.24) (PDF p. 29-30), ONATE2 (5.21)-(5.23) (PDF p. 272-273). The sources use a small element of the plate, we a finite piece. Named after Germain and Lagrange: TIMO PDF p. 128, VK PDF p. 30 ascribes the equation to Lagrange.

The operator \(\nabla^4 = \nabla^2\nabla^2\) is the biharmonic operator: \(\nabla^2\) is the Laplace operator (definition 11.5), after which the harmonic functions with \(\nabla^2 f = 0\) are named, and \(\nabla^4\) applies it twice, hence the prefix bi-. Equation (18.17) is the plate equation, abroad often called the Germain-Lagrange equation after the people in the story above. Per unit width of a beam, with \(w = w(x)\), it reduces to \(D\,w'''' = q\), which is the deflection curve equation (theorem 5.42) with \(EI\) replaced by \(D\).

Let us test the theorem on the field of the previous section. For \(w = q\,(x^4 + y^4)/(48\,D)\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = w_{\mathrm{yyyy}} = 24\,q/(48\,D) = q/(2D)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xxyy}} = 0\), so \(D\,\nabla^4 w = q\). Its \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -D\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\nabla^2 w = -D\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\,\big(q\,(x^2 + y^2)/(4D)\big) = -q\,x/2\), which agrees with the previous example, where the transverse forces balanced the load.

18.2.4 Germain's energy: the same equation, a different energy

The story said that Germain got the correct equation from a wrong energy. Let us see what this means. Her energy, written with the same constant \(D/2\) as the correct one, is \(\tfrac{D}{2}\int (\nabla^2 w)^2\,\mathrm{d}A\): the sum of the curvatures in two perpendicular directions, \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{yy}}\), which does not depend on the choice of axes, squared. The correct energy, which we shall derive in section 18.3, has in the square bracket one more term, \(-2(1 - \nu)(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{yy}} - w_{\mathrm{xy}}^2)\). That the equation cannot tell the two apart is due to this term. Its integral can be written with edge terms alone, as section 18.3 will show (lemma 18.18), so it does not change the equation in the interior. In derivatives this shows as \(\partial^2(w_{\mathrm{yy}})/\partial x^2 - 2\,\partial^2(w_{\mathrm{xy}})/\partial x\,\partial y + \partial^2(w_{\mathrm{xx}})/\partial y^2 = w_{\mathrm{xxyy}} - 2\,w_{\mathrm{xxyy}} + w_{\mathrm{xxyy}} = 0\) for a four times continuously differentiable \(w\) (theorem 8.30). The two energies are told apart by the edge and by the value of the energy itself.

We can do the experiment ourselves. Take a flat plate of cardboard, dashed in the figure, and hold it by the four corners: two diagonal ones up and two down. The plate twists into the surface \(w = c\,x\,y\), in which every mesh line is straight. Everywhere \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = w_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), so \(\nabla^2 w = 0\), and Germain's energy is zero. But we cannot twist the plate without the forces \(F\) at the corners. The correct energy has the density \(\tfrac{D}{2}\cdot 2(1 - \nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 = D(1 - \nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\), which is not zero. At \(w_{\mathrm{xy}} = c = 0{,}01\) 1/m we have \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = D(1 - \nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xy}} = 125{,}64\) N m/m and the correct energy per unit area is \(1{,}256\) J/m², Germain's is zero (SymPy). Equation (18.17) for this \(w\) says \(0 = q\) and it holds, because there is no load in the interior. The equation therefore does not see the twist, because its work is at the edge, where the moment \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is carried by the forces \(F\) at the corners. How, section 18.3 shows.

The equation is the same for both energies, so it cannot tell them apart. The edge conditions we need for the problem to be solvable we shall get from the correct energy in section 18.3. That the equation does not determine the correct energy is therefore a warning: agreement of the equation does not prove the energy.

18.2.5 Shear stress through the thickness

The third question is still waiting. In the Kirchhoff model the shear strains \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero by definition, so the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) cannot be obtained from Hooke's law, yet the transverse force \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} \ne 0\) is, as we saw, necessary. This is the same contradiction as for the beam (section 5.3.4). The remedy is the same too: we get the stress from equilibrium, not from the strain.

Lemma 18.13 Shear stresses through the thickness of a plate (strižne napetosti po debelini plošče)

Let the plate be as in theorem 18.12, without body forces, with continuous derivatives of the stresses, and let both surfaces carry no tangential load (\(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\) at \(z = \pm h/2\)). Then

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \frac{3\,Q_{\mathrm{x}}}{2h}\Big( 1 - \frac{4z^2}{h^2} \Big) , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \frac{3\,Q_{\mathrm{y}}}{2h}\Big( 1 - \frac{4z^2}{h^2} \Big) . \tag{18.19}\]

The largest value is \(\tfrac{3}{2}\,Q_{\mathrm{x}}/h\) at \(z = 0\), that is one and a half times the mean.

Proof

We must show the form of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) in \(z\) at every \((x, y)\). We use the equilibrium equation in the direction \(x\) and the known normal stresses.

  1. The stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are linear in \(z\) (Hooke's law in plane stress for the strains \(-z\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(-z\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}\), theorem 18.7): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = z\,s_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = z\,s_{\mathrm{xy}}\) with coefficients independent of \(z\). From the definition \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -\int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}z = -s_{\mathrm{x}}\,h^3/12\) we get \(s_{\mathrm{x}} = -12\,M_{\mathrm{x}}/h^3\), and likewise \(s_{\mathrm{xy}} = -12\,M_{\mathrm{xy}}/h^3\).
  2. The first equilibrium equation ((2.31)) without body forces is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx},\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx},\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx},\mathrm{z}} = 0\), with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) (theorem 2.36). So \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z = -z\,(s_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + s_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}}) = 12\,z\,(M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}})/h^3\).
  3. By equation (18.16) \(M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}} = -Q_{\mathrm{x}}\) (step 3 of the proof of theorem 18.12). Hence \(\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/\partial z = -12\,z\,Q_{\mathrm{x}}/h^3\).
  4. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -6\,Q_{\mathrm{x}}\,z^2/h^3 + c(x, y)\).
  5. On the surface \(z = h/2\) the normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and by Cauchy's formula \(t_{\mathrm{x}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), which is zero by assumption. So \(c = 6\,Q_{\mathrm{x}}\,(h/2)^2/h^3 = 3\,Q_{\mathrm{x}}/(2h)\). The surface \(z = -h/2\) gives the same value of \(c\), since \(z^2\) is the same there. This gives the first equation (18.19). We get the second by exchanging \(x\) and \(y\).
  6. Check: \(\int_{-\mathrm{h}/2}^{h/2}\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}z = \tfrac{3Q_{\mathrm{x}}}{2h}\big(h - \tfrac{4}{h^2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}\,(\tfrac{h}{2})^3\big) = \tfrac{3Q_{\mathrm{x}}}{2h}\cdot\tfrac{2h}{3} = Q_{\mathrm{x}}\), as definition 18.9 demands.

Source: VK (2.16) (PDF p. 28) gives the same parabola through the thickness, written there with \(\nabla^2 w\), and notes that \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) vary by a parabolic law. The proof is ours, with the same step as theorem 5.39 for the beam.

We read the figure like this. On the cut face the thickness \(h\) is vertical. The normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) grows linearly with the distance from the middle plane and gives a pair of forces, the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\). The shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is zero at both surfaces, because the surface is free, and is largest in the middle, and its sum is \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\).

Let us try an example. A square plate \(a = 500\) mm, \(h = 10\) mm, simply supported on all edges, under \(q = 10\) kPa (section 18.5) has at its centre \(|M_{\mathrm{x}}| = 119{,}72\) N m/m and the normal stress \(6\,|M_{\mathrm{x}}|/h^2 = 7{,}183\) MPa. The transverse force at the middle of an edge is \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}3376\,q\,a = 1688\) N/m (series, SymPy), so by the lemma \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 1{,}5 \cdot 1688/0{,}01 = 0{,}253\) MPa. The ratio is \(0{,}035\). Both stresses are proportional to the load, so the ratio is \(\tfrac{1{,}5 \cdot 0{,}3376}{6 \cdot 0{,}04789}\,h/a = 1{,}76\,h/a\), where \(0{,}3376\) and \(0{,}04789\) are the coefficients of the two series, \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}3376\,q\,a\) and \(|M_{\mathrm{x}}| = 0{,}04789\,q\,a^2\) (NumPy). The corresponding strains are the normal \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E = 3{,}67 \cdot 10^{-5}\) and the shear \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}/G = 3{,}36 \cdot 10^{-6}\), which the model neglects. The shear strain is therefore \(9\,\%\) of the normal one. More important is the energy, which carries the square of the stress: the density of shear energy \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}^2/(2G)\) against the density of normal energy \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2/(2E)\) is only \((1{,}76\,h/a)^2 \cdot E/G = (1{,}76\,h/a)^2 \cdot 2(1 + \nu) = 3{,}2 \cdot 10^{-3}\). This is an estimate by the largest densities, which lie at different points, the centre and the middle of an edge, so it does not give the total energy. The total effect on the deflection is computed in section 18.8: at \(a/h = 50\) the deflection computed with the shear strain is only \(1{,}0021\) times the Kirchhoff one. Since the ratio of the densities grows with the square of \(h/a\), at \(a/h = 5\) it would be a hundred times larger, about \(0{,}3\), and the Kirchhoff model is no longer good: there the deflection with the shear strain is \(1{,}2073\) times larger.

Let us sum up. A piece of plate needs the transverse forces \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\) because the moment pairs cannot carry the load (lemma 18.10). From the equilibrium of a piece and the divergence theorem in the plane follows \(D\,\nabla^4 w = q\) (theorem 18.12), and from the equilibrium equation at a point the parabolic shear stress (lemma 18.13). The same equation also follows from a wrong energy, so the equation alone does not determine the edge conditions we need for a solution. That is the work of the next section.

18.3 Energy, boundary conditions and uniqueness of a plate

We obtained the plate equation \(D\,\nabla^4 w = q\) (theorem 18.12) from the equilibrium of a finite piece of the middle plane. The solution of a fourth-order equation is determined only when we say what happens at the edge of the plate, and the equilibrium of a piece in the interior does not say that. The beam was the same: the fourth-order equation had four free constants, the conditions at the ends fixed them, and theorem 5.69 showed that the first variation of the energy gives the equation and the conditions at once (section 5.11.4). Chapter 5 promised for plates that the divergence theorem replaces integration by parts. We ask three questions. Which energy does a plate have, and is it always non-negative? Which equation and which edge conditions follow from the stationarity of the energy? And do these conditions determine the deflection uniquely?

The answer will have the form the beam already knows, with one novelty. The edge of a plate is a curve and not a point, so there is also a rotation in the direction of the edge and with it a twisting moment \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which the beam does not have. We shall therefore have to find that at a free edge the transverse force and the twisting moment merge into one force, and that point forces appear at the corners.

18.3.1 Model and energy

Take a plate (definition 18.1) with a rectangular plan \(R = [0, a] \times [0, b]\) of the middle plane, of constant thickness \(h\), of a homogeneous isotropic material with modulus of elasticity \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) (definitions 3.1 and 3.2), where \(-1 < \nu < 1\). The deflection of the middle plane is \(w(x, y)\) and the load \(q(x, y)\) per unit area points in the direction of \(w\). The idealizations of the Kirchhoff plate hold (definition 18.2): the plate is thin, the deflection is small, the normals stay straight and perpendicular to the middle plane, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is neglected and every layer is in plane stress. The rectangle has four edges and four corners. For now there is no load on the edges, so the edges are either fixed or free (loaded edges are described by the remark after theorem 18.21). As an example we take the steel plate of the running example of the chapter: \(a = b = 500\) mm, \(h = 10\) mm, \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(D = 17\,948{,}7\) N m (definition 18.6) and \(q = 10\) kPa.

Let us write down what we know from section 18.1, in the same sign convention as for the beam (\(M = EI\,v''\), equation (5.24)). By theorem 18.7 the moments per unit length are

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\,(w_{\mathrm{xx}} + \nu\,w_{\mathrm{yy}}) , \qquad M_{\mathrm{y}} = D\,(w_{\mathrm{yy}} + \nu\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}) , \qquad M_{\mathrm{xy}} = D\,(1 - \nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xy}} , \tag{18.20}\]

and \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are by definition 18.5 the integrals \(-\int z\,\sigma\,\mathrm{d}z\) through the thickness, with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Below we also need the transverse forces \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -(M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}})\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{y}} = -(M_{\mathrm{y},\mathrm{y}} + M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{x}})\) (definition 18.9, the relation to the moments is the moment balance in the proof of theorem 18.12, steps 2 and 3), where an index after the comma means a partial derivative. The moments and transverse forces of a plate are per unit length of the edge (\(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) in N m/m, \(Q_{\mathrm{x}}\) in N/m), so they differ from \(M\) and \(V\) of a beam in N m and N.

The energy of a beam was the integral of the energy density over the body (definition 5.75). For a plate we take it from the same definition for the body \(V = R \times [-h/2, h/2]\) that the plate occupies (\(z\) is the coordinate perpendicular to the middle plane), and we write it with the deflection. That the integral below is indeed this energy is shown by lemma 18.15.

Definition 18.14 Strain energy of a plate (deformacijska energija plošče)

Let the plate be as above and \(w\) its deflection. The strain energy of the plate is the number

\[U(w) = \frac12 \int_{\mathrm{R}} D\,\big[ (\nabla^2 w)^2 - 2\,(1 - \nu)\,(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{yy}} - w_{\mathrm{xy}}^2) \big]\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{18.21}\]

where \(\nabla^2 w = w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(w\) has continuous derivatives up to second order on \(R\). It is a functional of the field \(w\): the input is a function \(w\) on \(R\) and the output is a number in joules.

Source: EP (7.2.90) (p. 430-431, written there with the moments). The form with \((1 - \nu)\) follows from it (lemma 18.15).

Why the energy has this form is shown by the next lemma. It also shows that it equals half the integral of the products of moments and curvatures, as for the beam \(\tfrac12\int M\,v''\,\mathrm{d}x\).

Lemma 18.15 Strain energy of a plate in terms of the moments (energija plošče iz momentov)

Under the idealizations of the Kirchhoff plate the strain energy of the body \(V = R \times [-h/2, h/2]\) with the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -z\,w_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = w\) (theorem 18.3) is

\[U = \frac12 \int_{\mathrm{R}} \big( M_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} + M_{\mathrm{y}}\,w_{\mathrm{yy}} + 2\,M_{\mathrm{xy}}\,w_{\mathrm{xy}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{18.22}\]

which equals (18.21).

Proof

We must show that the integral of the energy density through the thickness gives the moments, and that inserting the relations (18.20) gives (18.21).
