For the shear forces \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{mn}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{y}} = D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{mn}}\).

Proof

We must show that \(s_{\mathrm{mn}}\) is an eigenfunction of the operator \(\nabla^2\), from this \(\nabla^4\) follows, then the boundary conditions and the shear forces.

  1. By the theorem on derivatives of sine and cosine (8.12), \(\partial_{\mathrm{xx}}s_{\mathrm{mn}} = -(m\pi/a)^2 s_{\mathrm{mn}}\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{yy}}s_{\mathrm{mn}} = -(n\pi/b)^2 s_{\mathrm{mn}}\). The sum is \(\nabla^2 s_{\mathrm{mn}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}\,s_{\mathrm{mn}}\).
  2. The operator is linear, so \(\nabla^4 s_{\mathrm{mn}} = \nabla^2(-\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}s_{\mathrm{mn}}) = \lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2\,s_{\mathrm{mn}}\). For \(w_{\mathrm{mn}} = W_{\mathrm{mn}}s_{\mathrm{mn}}\) we get \(D\nabla^4 w_{\mathrm{mn}} = D\,W_{\mathrm{mn}}\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2\,s_{\mathrm{mn}} = q_{\mathrm{mn}}\,s_{\mathrm{mn}}\).
  3. At \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\), \(\sin(m\pi x/a) = 0\) (lemma 8.10, point 2), so \(w_{\mathrm{mn}} = 0\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{xx}}w_{\mathrm{mn}} = -(m\pi/a)^2 w_{\mathrm{mn}} = 0\). At \(y = 0\) and \(y = b\) likewise \(w_{\mathrm{mn}} = 0\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{yy}}w_{\mathrm{mn}} = 0\). These are the conditions (18.32).
  4. By equation (18.16) (in the form of the model above), \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -D\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\nabla^2 w_{\mathrm{mn}} = -D\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}(-\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}w_{\mathrm{mn}}) = D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{mn}}\), and likewise for \(Q_{\mathrm{y}}\).

Source: EP section 7.2.4 (printed pp. 436-438) inserts the double sine series into the plate equation and obtains the equation for the coefficients \(W_{\mathrm{mn}}\) (7.2.116-7.2.119). The proof by the eigenfunction of \(\nabla^2\) is ours, the idea is the same as for the beam in theorem 13.46.

The lemma holds for each term separately, but the load is usually a sum of infinitely many terms. For the beam we took the derivative of the series from the expansion theorem. Here we need a smaller theorem that says when we may differentiate a series term by term.

Lemma 18.29 Term by term differentiation of a series (odvajanje vrste člen za členom)

Let \(I\) be an interval, \(J\) an interval and \((u_{\mathrm{k}})\) a sequence of continuous functions \(I \times J \to \mathbb{R}\) whose partial derivative \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuous. Let \(M_{\mathrm{k}} = \sup|u_{\mathrm{k}}|\) and \(M_{\mathrm{k}}' = \sup|\partial_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{k}}|\) with \(\sum M_{\mathrm{k}} < \infty\) and \(\sum M_{\mathrm{k}}' < \infty\). Then the series \(F = \sum u_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(G = \sum \partial_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{k}}\) converge uniformly, \(F\) and \(G\) are continuous, the derivative \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}} F\) exists and equals \(G\). The same holds for \(\partial_{\mathrm{y}}\). For double indices \(k = (m, n)\) the sum does not depend on the order of the terms.

Proof

We must show uniform convergence, continuity of the limit and the exchange of derivative and sum. The first is Weierstrass's criterion, the second an estimate with \(\eta/3\), the third the fundamental theorem of calculus.

  1. By theorem 9.85 (points 1 and 2) the series converge absolutely and uniformly, so independently of the order. The sums are \(F\) and \(G\), the partial sums \(F_{\mathrm{N}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{N}}\).
  2. Let \(\eta > 0\). Choose \(N\) with \(\sup|F - F_{\mathrm{N}}| < \eta/3\). The function \(F_{\mathrm{N}}\) is continuous at the point \(p\), so there is \(\delta > 0\) with \(|F_{\mathrm{N}}(p') - F_{\mathrm{N}}(p)| < \eta/3\) for \(|p' - p| < \delta\). Then \(|F(p') - F(p)| \le |F(p') - F_{\mathrm{N}}(p')| + |F_{\mathrm{N}}(p') - F_{\mathrm{N}}(p)| + |F_{\mathrm{N}}(p) - F(p)| < \eta\). So \(F\) is continuous, and likewise \(G\).
  3. For every \(y\) and numbers \(x_0, x\), by the fundamental theorem of calculus (3.40, point 1) \(u_{\mathrm{k}}(x, y) - u_{\mathrm{k}}(x_0, y) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}\partial_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{k}}(s, y)\,\mathrm{d}s\). Summing the first \(N\) terms, \(F_{\mathrm{N}}(x, y) - F_{\mathrm{N}}(x_0, y) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}G_{\mathrm{N}}(s, y)\,\mathrm{d}s\). By the integral estimate lemma (9.31), \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}(G - G_{\mathrm{N}})\,\mathrm{d}s\big| \le |x - x_0|\sup|G - G_{\mathrm{N}}| \to 0\), so \(F(x, y) - F(x_0, y) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x}G(s, y)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  4. The function \(s \mapsto G(s, y)\) is continuous (step 2), so by the fundamental theorem (3.40, point 2) \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}} F(x, y) = G(x, y)\) exists.

Source: The theorem is standard, the proof is not from a source. The same idea with the fundamental theorem of calculus.

Now we can state the main theorem. The coefficient \(q_{\mathrm{mn}}\) is the average of the load with the sine: the factor \(4/(ab)\) is the reciprocal of \(\iint s_{\mathrm{mn}}^2\,\mathrm{d}A = ab/4\), which follows from the orthogonality of sines (lemma 9.87 with \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2a\), the product \(\sin^2\) is an even function). Navier's load is not every function. The coefficients \(q_{\mathrm{mn}}\) must not decay more slowly than \(1/(mn)\), which holds for a uniform load (the reason is in the corollary below), and the load must be the sum of its series in the sense of integrals over rectangles. For a double series this is the condition that for a single series is guaranteed by lemma 13.10, and here we prove it only for the uniform load.

Theorem 18.30 Navier's solution of the simply supported rectangular plate (Navierova rešitev prosto podprte pravokotne plošče)

Let \(P = [0, a] \times [0, b]\) be a plate with rigidity \(D\) and \(0 \le \nu < 1\), simply supported on all edges (conditions (18.32)), and \(q\) a load on \(P\). Let

\[q_{\mathrm{mn}} = \frac{4}{ab}\int_0^a\!\!\int_0^b q(x, y)\,s_{\mathrm{mn}}(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \tag{18.34}\]

and let (H1) \(|q_{\mathrm{mn}}| \le K/(mn)\) for all natural \(m, n\) and some constant \(K\), (H2) \(\displaystyle\iint_{\mathrm{R}} q\,\mathrm{d}A = \sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}}q_{\mathrm{mn}}\iint_{\mathrm{R}} s_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) for every rectangle \(R = [x_1, x_2] \times [y_1, y_2] \subset P\). Let \(w_{\mathrm{mn}} = W_{\mathrm{mn}}s_{\mathrm{mn}}\) with \(W_{\mathrm{mn}}\) from equation (18.33). Then:

  1. The series \(w = \sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}}w_{\mathrm{mn}}\) and all its partial derivatives up to third order, obtained term by term, converge uniformly on \(P\) and absolutely. The function \(w\) is three times continuously differentiable on \(P\), the moments are continuous and
    \[M_{\mathrm{x}} = D\sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}}W_{\mathrm{mn}}\Big[\Big(\frac{m\pi}{a}\Big)^2 + \nu\Big(\frac{n\pi}{b}\Big)^2\Big]s_{\mathrm{mn}} , \qquad M_{\mathrm{xy}} = -D(1 - \nu)\sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}}W_{\mathrm{mn}}\frac{m\pi}{a}\frac{n\pi}{b}\cos\frac{m\pi x}{a}\cos\frac{n\pi y}{b} , \tag{18.35}\]
    and \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) is like \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(m\pi/a\) and \(n\pi/b\) exchanged.
  2. The function \(w\) satisfies the boundary conditions (18.32).
  3. For every rectangle \(R \subset P\) the equilibrium of the piece holds,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{y}_1}^{y_2}\big[Q_{\mathrm{x}}(x_2, y) - Q_{\mathrm{x}}(x_1, y)\big]\mathrm{d}y + \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\big[Q_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y_2) - Q_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y_1)\big]\mathrm{d}x + \iint_{\mathrm{R}} q\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 . \tag{18.36}\]
Idea

Each term solves the equation for its part of the load (lemma 18.28). The sum may be differentiated term by term if the series of derivatives converge uniformly, and this we show by estimating the terms. The equilibrium (18.36) holds for every partial sum, and in the limit for the sum.

Proof

We must show the estimate of the terms, the differentiation, the boundary conditions and the equilibrium of the piece.

  1. Let \(\rho = \max(m, n)\). We have \(\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}} \ge c\,\rho^2\) with \(c = \pi^2/\max(a, b)^2\), so by hypothesis (H1) \(|W_{\mathrm{mn}}| \le K/(mn\,D\,c^2\rho^4)\). The term of a partial derivative of order \(i + j \le 3\) of \(w_{\mathrm{mn}}\) is in absolute value at most \(|W_{\mathrm{mn}}|(m\pi/a)^i(n\pi/b)^j \le C_1\rho^3|W_{\mathrm{mn}}| \le C\,/(mn\,\rho)\) with constants \(C_1\), \(C\) determined by \(a\), \(b\), \(D\), \(K\). Since \(\rho^2 \ge mn\), this is \(\le C\,(mn)^{-3/2}\).
  2. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k} \ge 1}k^{-3/2}\) is finite: for \(k \ge 2\), \(k^{-3/2} \le \int_{\mathrm{k}-1}^{k}s^{-3/2}\,\mathrm{d}s\), so the sum is \(\le 1 + \int_1^\infty s^{-3/2}\,\mathrm{d}s = 3\). Hence \(\sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}}(mn)^{-3/2} \le 9\), and by theorem 9.85 the series of all derivatives up to third order converge uniformly and absolutely. By lemma 18.29, applied successively to derivatives of order 0, 1 and 2, \(w\) is three times continuously differentiable and the derivatives are the sums of the derivative series. From \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = -D(w_{\mathrm{xx}} + \nu w_{\mathrm{yy}})\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\sum W_{\mathrm{mn}}(m\pi/a)^2 s_{\mathrm{mn}}\) formula (18.35) follows, likewise for \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = -D(1 - \nu)w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  3. Every term is zero at \(x = 0, a\) and \(y = 0, b\) together with \(\partial_{\mathrm{xx}}\) or \(\partial_{\mathrm{yy}}\) respectively (step 3 of lemma 18.28). Since the series for \(w\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{yy}}\) converge, these values are zero also for the sum, and \(M_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) because \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = w_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\) on the edge.
  4. Let \(w_{\mathrm{N}} = \sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n} \le \mathrm{N}}w_{\mathrm{mn}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{N}} = \sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n} \le \mathrm{N}}q_{\mathrm{mn}}s_{\mathrm{mn}}\). By lemma 18.28, \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}}Q_{\mathrm{x}} + \partial_{\mathrm{y}}Q_{\mathrm{y}} = -D\nabla^4 w_{\mathrm{N}} = -q_{\mathrm{N}}\) for the partial sum. By the fundamental theorem of calculus and the theorem on the order of integration (4.9), the sum of the first two integrals of equation (18.36) for \(w_{\mathrm{N}}\) equals \(\iint_{\mathrm{R}}(\partial_{\mathrm{x}}Q_{\mathrm{x}} + \partial_{\mathrm{y}}Q_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}A = -\iint_{\mathrm{R}} q_{\mathrm{N}}\,\mathrm{d}A\). So for \(w_{\mathrm{N}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{N}}\) the equilibrium holds.
  5. As \(N \to \infty\), \(Q_{\mathrm{x}} = -D\partial_{\mathrm{x}}(w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{yy}})\) (a sum of derivatives of third order) tends uniformly to its limit, so by the integral estimate lemma (9.31) the integrals over the sides of \(R\) converge. The right side: \(\iint_{\mathrm{R}} s_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) has absolute value at most \(\frac{2a}{m\pi}\cdot\frac{2b}{n\pi}\), so by (H1) \(\sum|q_{\mathrm{mn}}|\,\big|\iint_{\mathrm{R}} s_{\mathrm{mn}}\big| \le \frac{4abK}{\pi^2}\sum(mn)^{-2} < \infty\), and by (H2) \(\iint_{\mathrm{R}} q_{\mathrm{N}}\,\mathrm{d}A \to \iint_{\mathrm{R}} q\,\mathrm{d}A\). The limit of the equilibrium is equation (18.36).
Explanation

Equation (18.36) is the force equilibrium of every rectangular piece of the middle plane (lemma 18.10), which by the same argument as in that lemma (vanishing integrand, section 18.2) is replaced by the differential equation at points where the derivatives of fourth order are continuous. That \(w\) is the only solution this theorem does not claim: uniqueness is proved by theorem 18.23 for solutions in its class. Without it the theorem says that this \(w\) is a solution.

Source: EP section 7.2.4 (printed pp. 435-440): expansion of \(w\) and \(q\) into a double sine series, moments and shear forces (p. 439), formula (7.2.119). VK section 3.3 (PDF pp. 52-54) the same procedure, on convergence it says only that the series is estimated with \(|\sin| \le 1\) (PDF p. 54). The proof of convergence of derivatives, of term by term differentiation and of the equilibrium of the piece is ours. (H2) for a general load means completeness of the double sines and we do not prove it (assumption of completeness), we prove it for the uniform load.

How is the theorem used? From the load we compute the coefficients \(q_{\mathrm{mn}}\) by a double integral (equation (18.34)), divide each by \(D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2\), and put the result in front of the sine. For a uniform load all three steps are written in formulas.

Corollary 18.31 Uniform load on the simply supported rectangle (enakomerna obtežba prosto podprtega pravokotnika)

Let \(q = q_0\) be constant on \(P\). Then the hypotheses (H1) and (H2) are satisfied, \(q_{\mathrm{mn}} = 16q_0/(\pi^2 mn)\) for odd \(m\), \(n\) and \(q_{\mathrm{mn}} = 0\) otherwise, and

\[w(x, y) = \frac{16\,q_0}{\pi^6 D}\sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{mn\big(m^2/a^2 + n^2/b^2\big)^2}\,s_{\mathrm{mn}}(x, y) . \tag{18.37}\]

At the centre of the square \(a = b\), \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}004062\,q_0a^4/D\) and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = M_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}04789\,q_0a^2\). The number \(0{,}004062\) does not depend on \(\nu\) (\(\nu\) enters only through \(D\)), the number \(0{,}04789\) is computed at \(\nu = 0{,}3\).

Proof

We must show the coefficients, hypothesis (H1) and hypothesis (H2), the rest is theorem 18.30.

  1. For natural \(m\), \(\int_0^a\sin(m\pi x/a)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{a}{m\pi}(1 - \cos m\pi)\), which is \(\frac{2a}{m\pi}\) for odd \(m\) and \(0\) for even. From formula (18.34), \(q_{\mathrm{mn}} = \frac{4}{ab}q_0\cdot\frac{2a}{m\pi}\cdot\frac{2b}{n\pi} = \frac{16q_0}{\pi^2 mn}\) for odd \(m\), \(n\), otherwise zero. Hypothesis (H1) holds with \(K = 16q_0/\pi^2\).
  2. For (H2) let \(h(x) = x(a - x)/2\) on \([0, a]\). The function is piecewise continuously differentiable and \(h(0) = h(a) = 0\), so by lemma 13.10 \(h = \sum_{\mathrm{m}} h_{\mathrm{m}}\sin(m\pi x/a)\) uniformly, with \(h_{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{2}{a}\int_0^a h\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{4a^2}{\pi^3m^3}\) for odd \(m\) and \(0\) for even (SymPy).
  3. The series of derivatives \(\sum h_{\mathrm{m}}\frac{m\pi}{a}\cos\frac{m\pi x}{a} = \sum_{\mathrm{m}\ \text{odd}}\frac{4a}{\pi^2m^2}\cos\frac{m\pi x}{a}\) has terms of absolute value at most \(\frac{4a}{\pi^2m^2}\), and the series of sines \(\frac{4a^2}{\pi^3m^3}\), and both series of maxima converge, so by lemma 18.29 \(h'(x) = \frac{a - 2x}{2} = \sum_{\mathrm{m}\ \text{odd}}\frac{4a}{\pi^2m^2}\cos\frac{m\pi x}{a}\).
  4. For \(0 \le x_1 \le x_2 \le a\) we therefore have \(x_2 - x_1 = h'(x_1) - h'(x_2) = \sum_{\mathrm{m}\ \text{odd}}\frac{4a}{\pi^2m^2}\Big(\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{a} - \cos\frac{m\pi x_2}{a}\Big) = \sum_{\mathrm{m}\ \text{odd}}\frac{4}{m\pi}\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\sin(m\pi x/a)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{a}{m\pi}(\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{a} - \cos\frac{m\pi x_2}{a})\). The same for \(y\) with \(b\).
  5. The product of two absolutely convergent series is a double series, and by theorem 4.9 \(\iint_{\mathrm{R}} s_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{a}\,\mathrm{d}x\int_{\mathrm{y}_1}^{y_2}\sin\frac{n\pi y}{b}\,\mathrm{d}y\). Hence \(\sum q_{\mathrm{mn}}\iint_{\mathrm{R}} s_{\mathrm{mn}}\,\mathrm{d}A = q_0\big(\sum\frac{4}{m\pi}\int\sin\big)\big(\sum\frac{4}{n\pi}\int\sin\big) = q_0(x_2 - x_1)(y_2 - y_1) = \iint_{\mathrm{R}} q_0\,\mathrm{d}A\). This is (H2).
  6. Theorem 18.30 gives \(w = \sum q_{\mathrm{mn}}s_{\mathrm{mn}}/(D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2)\), which is equation (18.37), since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2 = \pi^4(m^2/a^2 + n^2/b^2)^2\) and \(16q_0/(\pi^2mn)\cdot 1/\pi^4 = 16q_0/(\pi^6mn)\). At the centre \(s_{\mathrm{mn}} = \sin(m\pi/2)\sin(n\pi/2) = \pm 1\). The sum with \(a = b\), computed up to \(N = 399\) (NumPy), gives \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}004062\,q_0a^4/D\) and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}04789\,q_0a^2\) with \(\nu = 0{,}3\).

Source: EP section 7.2.4 (printed p. 437, table 7.2.3) gives the coefficients for the uniform load, example 7.2.9 (pp. 441-442) and table 9.5.1 (p. 628) the same values \(0{,}4062\cdot 10^{-2}\) and \(0{,}4789\cdot 10^{-1}\) for the square at \(\nu = 0{,}3\). The proof of (H2) by the series for \(h(x) = x(a - x)/2\) is ours.

Let us test the corollary on the steel plate from the beginning. At \(q = 10\) kPa, \(q\,a^4/D = 10^4\cdot 0{,}5^4/17\,948{,}7 = 0{,}03482\) m, so the deflection at the centre is \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}004062\cdot 0{,}03482\) m \(= 0{,}1415\) mm. This is \(w_{\mathrm{c}}/h = 0{,}014\) of the thickness. The moment is \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}04789\cdot 10^4\cdot 0{,}25 = 119{,}72\) N m/m and the stress at the surface \(\sigma = 6M_{\mathrm{x}}/h^2 = 7{,}18\) MPa (corollary 18.8). The assumption \(w \ll h\) about the smallness of the deflection is needed because for a deflection comparable to the thickness the middle plane stretches: the stretch is of order \((w/a)^2\), the bending strain at the surface is of order \(h\,w/a^2\), the ratio of the two is of order \(w/h\), here \(0{,}014\), so the stretch is of the order of one percent of the bending. For deflections comparable to \(h\) only the theory of large deflections helps, which section 18.10 merely names.

How many terms do we need? The table gives the partial sums with \(m, n \le N\) at the centre of the square.

\(N\) terms \(w_{\mathrm{c}}\,D/(q_0a^4)\) error of \(w\) \(M_{\mathrm{x}}/(q_0a^2)\) error of \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\)
1 1 0,004161 2,42 % 0,05338 11,48 %
3 4 0,004055 0,17 % 0,04692 2,01 %
5 9 0,004064 0,03 % 0,04823 0,73 %
11 36 0,004062 below 0,01 % 0,04784 0,10 %
21 121 0,004062 below 0,01 % 0,04789 0,02 %

The first term alone (\(m = n = 1\)) gives \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 4/\pi^6 = 0{,}004161\) and \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = 4(1 + \nu)/\pi^4 = 0{,}05338\) in the units \(q_0a^4/D\) and \(q_0a^2\). The moment converges more slowly than the deflection for a reason the formula shows: the coefficient of the deflection decays as \(1/(mn(m^2 + n^2)^2)\), the coefficient of the moment as \(1/(mn(m^2 + n^2))\), because differentiating twice multiplies a term by \((m\pi/a)^2\) or \((n\pi/b)^2\). So the second term (\(m = 1\), \(n = 3\)) is \(-1{,}3\) % of the first for the deflection and \(-3{,}8\) % for the moment (NumPy). The signs of the terms alternate, so the partial sums of the moment oscillate about the limit (0,04692 below it, 0,04823 above it).

Figure 18.15 shows this in two parts. On the left axis is \(N\), on the vertical one the error in percent. Both curves fall: the blue one for the deflection faster, the orange one for the moment more slowly, but in both cases towards zero. The right half is another case, the point load, and we shall draw it further on.

Navier's series also covers rectangles that are not squares. The ratio of sides \(b/a\) enters only \(\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}\). The table gives the values at the centre for \(b/a = 1, \dots, 5\), in the units \(q_0a^4/D\) and \(q_0a^2\), and the comparison with the strip of section 18.4, which has \(5/384 = 0{,}013021\) and \(M = 1/8\).

\(b/a\) \(w_{\mathrm{c}}\,D/(q_0a^4)\) \(M_{\mathrm{x}}/(q_0a^2)\) \(M_{\mathrm{y}}/(q_0a^2)\) \(w_{\mathrm{c}}\) relative to strip \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) relative to strip
1 0,004062 0,04789 0,04789 0,312 0,383
1,5 0,007724 0,08116 0,04984 0,593 0,649
2 0,010129 0,10168 0,04635 0,778 0,813
3 0,012233 0,11886 0,04063 0,940 0,951
5 0,012971 0,12462 0,03775 0,996 0,997

At \(b/a = 5\) the deflection differs from the strip by \(0{,}4\) %, and the moment \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) is \(0{,}03775\) while the strip has \(\nu/8 = 0{,}0375\) (in a long plate bending in the direction \(y\) occurs only through the transverse strain, \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = \nu M_{\mathrm{x}}\)). A plate longer than three widths is therefore already a strip to within about \(6\) %: far from the short edges the plate bends in one direction. The square is \(3{,}2\) times less flexible than a strip of the same width (\(0{,}004062\) against \(0{,}013021\)), because it carries the load in both directions. If it were carried by two crossed strips, each with half, the deflection would be \(0{,}013021/2 = 0{,}00651\), which is still \(60\) % too much. The difference is added by the twisting moment \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which strips lack (section 18.1). We check this on a plate without it: with \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) the equilibrium is \(D(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + 2\nu w_{\mathrm{xxyy}} + w_{\mathrm{yyyy}}) = q\), and Navier's series with the denominator \(m^4 + 2\nu m^2n^2 + n^4\) instead of \((m^2 + n^2)^2\) gives \(0{,}006290\,q_0a^4/D\) at the centre (NumPy), \(55\) % more than the plate and close to the estimate with two crossed strips.

A uniform load on a simply supported plate gives more than deflection and moment. The corners show something that the beam does not have.

Corollary 18.32 Corner forces of the simply supported square (vogalne sile prosto podprtega kvadrata)

Under a uniform load \(q_0\) of a simply supported square with side \(a\), every corner carries the force \(R = 2(1 - \nu)\,D\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0)\), and

\[R = \frac{32(1 - \nu)}{\pi^4}\,q_0a^2\sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}\ \text{odd}}\frac{1}{(m^2 + n^2)^2} = 0{,}06496\,q_0a^2 . \tag{18.38}\]

The support must pull it down. At \(q_0 = 10\) kPa and \(a = 500\) mm, \(R = 162{,}4\) N, the four corners together \(649{,}6\) N, which is \(26{,}0\) % of the total load \(q_0a^2 = 2500\) N.

Proof

We must show the value of \(w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) in the corner, then the force by the corollary on the corner force and the equilibrium of the whole plate.

  1. By theorem 18.30, \(w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the sum of a series with terms \(W_{\mathrm{mn}}\frac{m\pi}{a}\frac{n\pi}{b}\cos\frac{m\pi x}{a}\cos\frac{n\pi y}{b}\). In the corner \((0, 0)\) both cosines are \(1\) and all terms are positive. For \(a = b\) and \(q_{\mathrm{mn}} = 16q_0/(\pi^2mn)\) the term is \(\frac{16q_0}{\pi^2 mn D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2mn}{a^2} = \frac{16q_0}{D\,a^2\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2}\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}} = \pi^2(m^2 + n^2)/a^2\). The sum is \(w_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0) = \frac{16q_0a^2}{\pi^4D}\sum\frac{1}{(m^2 + n^2)^2}\), and \(D\) cancels in \(R\).
  2. By corollary 18.22 the support holds the corner \((0, 0)\) with the force \(F_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\,M_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0)\) in the direction of the axis \(z\), that is upward. The outward normals of the edges \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = -1\), so \(F_{\mathrm{c}} = 2M_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0)\). By formula (18.35), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0) = -D(1 - \nu)w_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0)\), and \(w_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0) > 0\) by step 1. So \(F_{\mathrm{c}} = -2(1 - \nu)Dw_{\mathrm{xy}}(0, 0) = -R\): a force of magnitude \(R\) pointing down. Hence formula (18.38). The series \(\sum(m^2 + n^2)^{-2}\) over odd \(m\), \(n\) has the sum \(0{,}2825\) (NumPy up to \(N = 3999\)), so \(R = 32\cdot 0{,}7/\pi^4\cdot 0{,}2825\,q_0a^2 = 0{,}06496\,q_0a^2\).
  3. The check is the equilibrium of vertical forces of the whole plate. The load is \(q_0a^2\) downward. By the same corollary the support holds the edge \(x = 0\) (\(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\)) with the force \(V_{\mathrm{n}} = M_{\mathrm{x},\mathrm{x}} + 2M_{\mathrm{xy},\mathrm{y}}\) per unit length in the direction of the axis \(z\) (definition 18.19), with our moments \(V_{\mathrm{n}} = -D\,[w_{\mathrm{xxx}} + (2 - \nu)w_{\mathrm{xyy}}]\), and by theorem 18.30 this is \(D\sum W_{\mathrm{mn}}\frac{m\pi}{a}\big[(m\pi/a)^2 + (2 - \nu)(n\pi/a)^2\big]\sin\frac{n\pi y}{a}\). Its integral along the edge is \(0{,}3149\,q_0a^2\) (NumPy, \(N = 3999\)), over the four edges \(1{,}2597\,q_0a^2\), and this is \(q_0a^2 + 4R = 1{,}2599\,q_0a^2\) (the difference \(0{,}0002\) is the remainder of the truncated series), as equation (18.29) requires with the load \(-q_0\) in the direction of the axis \(z\). The sum is positive, so the support pushes the edge up. The edges together carry more than the load, and the corners pull down: if the corners were free, they would lift.

Source: EP section 7.2.4 (printed pp. 439-440) gives the reactions \(V_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(V_{\mathrm{y}}\) and the corner force \(2M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) of the same forms. The value \(0{,}0650\,q_0a^2\) for the square and the equilibrium are ours, checked with NumPy.

A force must be seen. Let us look at the edge \(x = 0\) from the side.

The edge is drawn as a horizontal line, of length \(a\). Under a uniform load the support pushes it up, so the arrows end on the edge. We divide the edge into ten pieces of length \(a/10\) and each piece carries its own force, the integral of the reaction \(V_{\mathrm{n}}\) over the piece. The force is largest at the middle of the edge (\(0{,}0417\,q_0a^2\)) and smallest at the corner (\(0{,}0131\,q_0a^2\)): the load near the corner is shared by the two edges that meet there, while the corner force carries none of it, since it pulls down like the load. If each edge carried only a quarter of the load, the force per piece would be \(0{,}025\,q_0a^2\), the middle carries \(1{,}7\) times more. In every corner the support pulls down with the force \(0{,}0650\,q_0a^2\), the arrow starts in the corner. By corollary 18.22 this force is the twisting moment \(M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) along the edge, replaced by pairs of vertical forces (section 18.3).

So far all examples satisfied (H1). Navier tested one more case, a load concentrated at a point.

Lemma 18.33 Point load at the centre of the square: the series of the moment diverges (točkovna sila v sredini kvadrata: vrsta za moment ne konvergira)

Let the simply supported square \([0, a]^2\) carry a force \(P\) at the centre, which is the limit of a load spread over an ever smaller circle. Its coefficients are \(q_{\mathrm{mn}} = \frac{4P}{a^2}\sin\frac{m\pi}{2}\sin\frac{n\pi}{2}\), so \(|q_{\mathrm{mn}}| = 4P/a^2\) for odd \(m\), \(n\), which does not satisfy (H1). Then:

  1. The series for \(w\) in equation (18.33) converges uniformly, \(w\) is continuous and \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}011601\,Pa^2/D\).
  2. The partial sums \(\sum_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n} \le \mathrm{N}}\) of the series for \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) at the centre are positive and grow beyond every bound as \(N \to \infty\).
Proof

We must show an estimate for \(w\) and a lower bound for the sum of the moment by blocks.

  1. For \(w\) the term is \(|W_{\mathrm{mn}}| = 4P/(a^2D\lambda_{\mathrm{mn}}^2) = 4Pa^2/(\pi^4D(m^2 + n^2)^2) \le 4Pa^2/(4\pi^4Dm^2n^2)\) because \((m^2 + n^2)^2 \ge 4m^2n^2\). The sum \(\sum(mn)^{-2}\) is finite, and by theorem 9.85 the series converges uniformly, its sum is continuous (step 2 of lemma 18.29). The sum at the centre is \(0{,}011601\,Pa^2/D\) (NumPy up to \(N = 1199\)).
  2. At the centre \(s_{\mathrm{mn}} = \pm1\), so the term of the series for \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) by formula (18.35) for odd \(m\), \(n\) is \(\frac{4P}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{m^2 + \nu n^2}{(m^2 + n^2)^2}\). The sign is plus because \(W_{\mathrm{mn}}\) has the sign of \(q_{\mathrm{mn}}\), that is \(\sin\frac{m\pi}{2}\sin\frac{n\pi}{2}\), and at the centre it is multiplied by \(s_{\mathrm{mn}}\) with the same sign. So the partial sums grow with \(N\). The indices \(m, n \le N\) form a square that the swap \(m \leftrightarrow n\) maps onto itself, so the sum with the numerator \(n^2 + \nu m^2\) has the same value. The average of both gives the partial sum \(\frac{2(1 + \nu)P}{\pi^2}\sum\frac{1}{m^2 + n^2}\) over odd \(m, n \le N\) (NumPy at \(N = 41\) gives \(0{,}4406\,P\) both ways).
  3. For \(k \ge 1\) let the block \(B_{\mathrm{k}}\) contain the odd \(m\), \(n\) from \((2^k, 2^{k+1}]\). There are \(2^{k-1}\) odd numbers in \((2^k, 2^{k+1}]\), so \(4^{k-1}\) pairs, and each has \(m^2 + n^2 \le 2\cdot 4^{k+1}\) and \(\frac{1}{m^2 + n^2} \ge \frac{1}{2\cdot4^{k+1}}\). Every block contributes to the sum \(\sum 1/(m^2 + n^2)\) at least \(\frac{4^{k-1}}{2\cdot 4^{k+1}} = \frac{1}{32}\). The blocks are disjoint and all in \(m, n \le 2^K\) for \(k < K\), so the partial sum of the moment at \(N = 2^K\) is at least \(\frac{2(1 + \nu)P}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{K - 1}{32} = (K - 1)\,\frac{(1 + \nu)P}{16\pi^2}\), which tends to infinity, also at \(\nu = 0\).

Source: VK section 3.4 (PDF p. 61) says that the series for moments, shear forces and stresses under a point load diverge at the singular point. Navier treated this case (TIMO PDF p. 130). The proof by blocks is ours.

The numbers show how slowly. At \(a = 500\) mm the partial sums of \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) at \(N = 11\), \(41\), \(161\), \(641\) are \(0{,}311\,P\), \(0{,}441\,P\), \(0{,}580\,P\), \(0{,}723\,P\). Every fourfold increase of \(N\) adds about \(0{,}13\) to \(0{,}14\,P\), that is \(0{,}093\), \(0{,}101\) and \(0{,}103\,P\) per \(\ln 4\), and the coefficient \((1 + \nu)/(4\pi) = 0{,}1035\) from section 18.6, where we treat the point load on the circular plate, has the same growth. The moment therefore grows as \(\ln N\). The deflection, on the other hand, converges fast: the partial sum at \(N = 3\) is \(0{,}967\) of the limit, at \(N = 11\) \(0{,}996\). Let us look at the right part of figure 18.15. On the right axis is again \(N\) on a logarithmic scale, vertically \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) in the unit \(P\). The points lie on an almost straight line, every multiple of four of \(N\) raises them by the same step, and the line does not reach the horizontal.

Why does the plate itself not have this? A series with \(N\) terms distinguishes positions at a distance of about \(a/N\): at \(N = 41\) this is \(12\) mm, at \(N = 161\) \(3\) mm. A real plate with \(h = 10\) mm is under the Kirchhoff assumptions only where \(w\) changes over lengths much larger than \(h\). A point load is an idealization of a force acting on a small area, and the plate theory under it does not hold at a distance of a few \(h\), because of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which it neglects, and because of the straight normals. At \(h = 10\) mm about \(N \approx 10\) terms make sense (\(a/N = 50\) mm, that is \(5h\)), at which the partial sum lies between \(0{,}29\,P\) (\(N = 9\)) and \(0{,}31\,P\) (\(N = 11\)). A sum with more terms is a pretty mathematical object, not a prediction of stress. The deflection is therefore a good result of a point load, the moment only at a distance from the force.

Navier thus solved both cases correctly, but the second demanded more than the theorem: the deflection at the point of the load is finite, the moment under the force is infinite for an ideal force. We shall find the same \(\ln\) for the circular plate (section 18.6), where we can sum it in closed form.

If only two opposite edges are simply supported, for example \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\), Navier's series does not fit the other two edges, because \(\sin(n\pi y/b)\) cannot satisfy a clamped edge \(w_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). A solution with a single series, in which the factor in \(y\) has a form adapted to the boundary condition, is Lévy's solution (EP section 7.2.5, printed pp. 449-454, VK section 3.5, PDF p. 65, where the year is 1900). We do not prove this solution and do not need it in this book.

What we have shown. We expanded the deflection and the load into products of sines, which satisfy the boundary conditions of the simply supported rectangle by themselves and are eigenfunctions of \(\nabla^4\) (lemma 18.28), so every term solves the equation for its part of the load. That the sum solves the equation as the equilibrium of every rectangular piece (theorem 18.30) we proved by estimating the terms, which guarantees uniform convergence of derivatives up to third order if the coefficients of the load do not decay more slowly than \(1/(mn)\). For the uniform load we proved this to the end (corollary 18.31) and computed the deflection, moment and stress of the steel plate, the corner forces (corollary 18.32) and the test against the strip from section 18.4. For the point load the hypothesis fails, and with it the series for the moment (lemma 18.33). Double sines will come once more in section 18.7, where they will be the modes of vibration of the simply supported plate, and the theorem on term by term differentiation will be needed there again.

18.6 Circular plates

The bottom of a pressurised vessel, a manhole cover, a pump membrane and a turbine disc share one property: their middle plane is a circle (VK, PDF p. 100). Such a plate is called a circular plate (krožna plošča), after the shape of its middle plane, a circle of radius \(a\). The square plate of section 18.5 needed a double series, but for the circle there is a hope that the computation simplifies a great deal: a circle looks the same from every side, so its solution should be the same too, if the load and the support do not change along the rim. Let us see what this says, and whether the computation is really so simple.

The model is the plate of sections 18.1 to 18.3, that is the Kirchhoff plate (definition 18.2) with its named idealizations: the plate is thin, its deflection is small compared with the thickness, the normals of the middle plane stay straight and perpendicular to it, and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is neglected. The running example is the circle inscribed in the square of example B of section 18.5: a steel plate of radius \(a = 250\) mm and thickness \(h = 10\) mm (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)) is loaded by a uniform pressure \(q = 10\) kPa that acts in the same direction as the displacement \(w\). The bending stiffness is \(D = E h^3/(12(1-\nu^2)) = 17\,948{,}7\) N m (definition 18.6). The idealizations have a measure: the ratio is \(h/a = 0{,}04\), that is \(2a/h = 50\). EP (p. 392) calls a plate thin if the ratio of its smallest in-plane dimension to the thickness is at least \(20\), and the largest displacement (of the simply supported plate) will be \(0{,}139\) mm, which is \(1{,}4\ \%\) of the thickness, so indeed much less than \(h\).

From history

Poisson rewrote the plate equation in polar coordinates for a load that depends only on the radius and gave a complete solution of this problem, and then applied it to a uniform load for a simply supported and for a clamped edge (TIMO, PDF p. 121). The reason for this success is our reading: when everything depends on the radius alone, the equation in the plane becomes an ordinary differential equation in one variable, which can be integrated step by step.

We repeat Poisson's step: the plate equation of theorem 18.12 is written for a field that depends only on the radius \(r\) and is integrated. On the way we will see what must hold at the centre, and the boundary conditions fix the constants. We will test the result on our plate and then show what happens when the force acts at one point, where this condition at the centre no longer holds.

Let us draw what we will compute (figure 18.17). On the left is the plate seen from above, a circle of radius \(a\) with the origin at the centre. The radius \(r\) to a point is the length \(r\), the point has the angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal axis, and the radius \(a\) reaches the rim. At the point on the radius \(r\) we place two direction vectors: \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) points outward along the radius and \(\vek e_\theta\) perpendicular to it, along the circle of radius \(r\). With a dashed circle we mark the piece of plate that we will treat: a disc of radius \(r < a\). On the right is the section through the axis, with the thickness greatly exaggerated. The plate is supported at both ends, the load \(q\) acts on top, and the arrows end on the surface because the pressure presses on the plate. The vertical dashed lines show where we cut the disc out. Where we cut it out, the rest of the plate is replaced by what it exerts on the rim of the disc: the shear force \(Q_{\mathrm{r}}\) per unit length of the rim and the bending moment \(M_{\mathrm{r}}\) per unit length of the rim. Below the section are the displacement \(w\) and the radius \(r\) of the disc: \(w\) points downward, in the direction of the load. The arrows show how the force and the moment actually act under our load. The shear force carries the disc upward, against the load, and the moment bends it so that the top, loaded surface is compressed and the bottom one stretched. The sign is as in section 18.1: \(Q_{\mathrm{r}}\) is positive in the direction of \(w\), and a moment is positive for compression on the surface toward which \(w\) points, here the bottom one. Hence \(Q_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{r}}\) in the figure are negative, which the computation will confirm.

How do we express all the quantities with the radius? Section 18.2 gave us the plate equation \(D\nabla^4 w = q\) (theorem 18.12) and the third section the moments, shear forces and boundary conditions in Cartesian coordinates. We need two steps: the operator \(\nabla^2\) in polar coordinates (we computed it in chapter 11, corollary 11.18), and then the moments and the shear force in polar form. Both follow from the next lemma.

Lemma 18.34 An axisymmetric plate (osnosimetrična plošča)

Let \(w(x, y) = F(r)\) with \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), where \(F\) is a four times continuously differentiable function on the interval \(0 < r \le a\). We write \(F' = \mathrm{d}F/\mathrm{d}r\). Then:

  1. \(\nabla^2 w = F'' + F'/r = \frac1r\,(r F')'\) and \(\nabla^4 w = \frac1r\,\big(r\,(\nabla^2 w)'\big)'\).
  2. At the point \((r, 0)\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F''\), \(w_{\mathrm{yy}} = F'/r\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). Hence in local axes whose axis \(x\) points along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) (and axis \(y\) along \(\vek e_\theta\)) the moments per unit length are
    \[M_{\mathrm{r}} = D\Big(F'' + \nu\,\frac{F'}{r}\Big) , \qquad M_\theta = D\Big(\frac{F'}{r} + \nu\,F''\Big) , \qquad M_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0 , \tag{18.39}\]
    and the shear force is \(Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -D\,(\nabla^2 w)'\), \(Q_\theta = 0\).
Proof

We must show the form of the Laplace operator for fields without angular dependence and express the second derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) at a point on the axis \(x\) with derivatives of the function \(F\).

  1. The function \(w\) does not depend on \(\theta\) and \(z\), so in corollary 11.18 the terms with derivatives in \(\theta\) and \(z\) vanish and \(\nabla^2 w = F'' + F'/r\). Since \((rF')' = F' + rF''\), this equals \(\frac1r(rF')'\).
  2. The function \(\psi = \nabla^2 w\) again depends only on \(r\) and is twice continuously differentiable, because \(F\) is four times. Corollary 11.18 applied to \(\psi\) gives \(\nabla^4 w = \nabla^2\psi = \frac1r(r\psi')'\). This is item 1.
  3. With \(\rho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) we have \(\partial\rho/\partial x = x/\rho\) and \(\partial\rho/\partial y = y/\rho\). The chain rule gives \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = F'\,x/\rho\) and
    \[w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F''\,\frac{x^2}{\rho^2} + F'\Big(\frac1\rho - \frac{x^2}{\rho^3}\Big) , \qquad w_{\mathrm{yy}} = F''\,\frac{y^2}{\rho^2} + F'\Big(\frac1\rho - \frac{y^2}{\rho^3}\Big) , \qquad w_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Big(F'' - \frac{F'}{\rho}\Big)\frac{xy}{\rho^2} .\]
  4. At the point \((r, 0)\) we have \(y = 0\), \(x = \rho = r\). Substituting: \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F''\), \(w_{\mathrm{yy}} = F'/r\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\).
  5. The function \(w\) depends only on the distance from the centre, so it does not change when the axes are rotated about the centre. Every point at the distance \(r\) can therefore be treated as the point \((r, 0)\) in rotated axes whose axis \(x\) points along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). Theorem 18.7 with \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = w_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{xy}} = w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) gives \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = D(w_{\mathrm{xx}} + \nu w_{\mathrm{yy}})\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = D(w_{\mathrm{yy}} + \nu w_{\mathrm{xx}})\), \(M_{\mathrm{xy}} = D(1-\nu)\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and with step 4 equations (18.39).
  6. By theorem 18.12 the shear force is \(\vek Q = -D\,\nabla(\nabla^2 w)\), that is the gradient of a function of \(r\) alone, so it points along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), and its component along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) is \(-D\,(\nabla^2 w)'\).

Source: EP (pp. 405-406, equations (7.2.32) to (7.2.37)) gives the equation, stresses, moments and shear force for an axisymmetric circular plate, VK (PDF p. 101) derives the Laplace operator in polar coordinates with the derivative rule. The proof with corollary 11.18 and the moments from the Cartesian form is not from the source.

Lemma 18.34 says that the plate equation for a field depending on \(r\) alone is an ordinary equation of fourth order. Before integrating, one more question: why should the solution for the circle really depend on \(r\) alone? The load and the support do not change along the rim, so a rotation about the centre leaves them unchanged. If we find a field \(w(r)\) that solves the equation and the boundary conditions, it is by theorem 18.23 the only solution, so a field that would depend on \(\theta\) as well is excluded. The uniqueness theorem thus spares us the question whether the solution is axisymmetric: it is enough to find it.

How do we solve the equation? The first integration will give the equilibrium of the disc of figure 18.17: the load on the disc is just the integral of the load, and the constant that appears in the integration will be a point force at the centre. The other three integrations give the displacement.

Theorem 18.35 An axisymmetric circular plate (osnosimetrična krožna plošča)

Let a circular plate of radius \(a\) be loaded by a load per unit area \(q(r)\) that is a continuous function on \([0, a]\), and let \(w(r)\) be a displacement, four times continuously differentiable on \(0 < r \le a\), that solves the equation \(D\nabla^4 w = q\) (theorem 18.12). Denote

\[\Phi(r) = \frac1D\int_0^r s\,q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]

Then:

  1. There exist constants \(c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4\) and a function \(w_{\mathrm{p}}\) (a particular solution) such that
    \[w(r) = w_{\mathrm{p}}(r) + c_1 + c_2 r^2 + c_3\ln r + c_4\,r^2\ln r . \tag{18.40}\]
    For a uniform load \(q_0\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = q_0 r^4/(64D)\).
  2. For every \(r > 0\) we have \(2\pi r\,Q_{\mathrm{r}}(r) + \int_0^r q(s)\,2\pi s\,\mathrm{d}s = -8\pi D\,c_4\). The left side is the sum of the forces in the direction of \(w\) on the disc of radius \(r\), the shear force along the rim and the load, as in equation (18.12) of lemma 18.10, which the same argument gives for the disc. Since the disc is in equilibrium, the right side is the negative of the point force at the centre. If there is no point force at the centre, \(c_4 = 0\), and if a force \(P\) acts in the direction of \(w\), \(c_4 = P/(8\pi D)\).
  3. If \(w\) is a continuously differentiable function of \(x\) and \(y\) also at the centre, then \(c_3 = 0\). A plate without a point force at the centre therefore has \(w = w_{\mathrm{p}} + c_1 + c_2 r^2\), two constants that the two boundary conditions at \(r = a\) determine.
Proof

We must show that the equation can be integrated four times and what the constants mean. Denote \(g = \nabla^2 w\).

  1. By lemma 18.34, \(g = \frac1r(rw')'\) and the equation is \(\frac1r(rg')' = q/D\), so \((rg')' = rq/D\).
  2. The function \(s\,q(s)\) is continuous, so \(\Phi\) is differentiable with \(\Phi' = rq/D\) by the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40). The difference \(rg' - \Phi\) has derivative zero, so it is a constant \(C_1\): \(rg' = \Phi + C_1\).
  3. We have \(g' = \Phi/r + C_1/r\). Let \(G(r) = \int_0^r \Phi(s)/s\,\mathrm{d}s\). Since \(\Phi(s) = O(s^2)\) as \(s \to 0\), \(\Phi/s\) is continuous and \(G\) is differentiable with \(G' = \Phi/r\). From \((\ln r)' = 1/r\) it follows that \(g = G + C_1\ln r + C_2\).
  4. Let \(H(r) = \int_0^r sG(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). From \((rw')' = rg\) and \((r^2\ln r/2 - r^2/4)' = r\ln r\) it follows that \(rw' = H + C_1\big(\tfrac12 r^2\ln r - \tfrac14 r^2\big) + \tfrac12 C_2 r^2 + C_3\).
  5. We divide by \(r\) and let \(K(r) = \int_0^r H(s)/s\,\mathrm{d}s\). Since \((\tfrac14 r^2\ln r - \tfrac14 r^2)' = \tfrac12 r\ln r - \tfrac14 r\), we get \(w = K + C_1\big(\tfrac14 r^2\ln r - \tfrac14 r^2\big) + \tfrac14 C_2 r^2 + C_3\ln r + C_4\). With \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = K\), \(c_1 = C_4\), \(c_2 = (C_2 - C_1)/4\), \(c_3 = C_3\), \(c_4 = C_1/4\) this is equation (18.40). For \(q = q_0\) we have \(\Phi = q_0r^2/(2D)\) and \(\nabla^2(r^4) = 16r^2\), \(\nabla^4(r^4) = 64\) (lemma 18.34), so \(D\nabla^4(q_0r^4/(64D)) = q_0\).
  6. For item 2: by lemma 18.34, \(Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -Dg'\), so \(2\pi rQ_{\mathrm{r}} = -2\pi D\,(\Phi + C_1)\). The term \(2\pi D\,\Phi(r) = \int_0^r q(s)\,2\pi s\,\mathrm{d}s\) is the load on the disc, so \(2\pi rQ_{\mathrm{r}} + \int_0^r q\,2\pi s\,\mathrm{d}s = -2\pi D\,C_1 = -8\pi D\,c_4\). If a force \(P\) also acts on the disc at the centre, the equilibrium of the disc by the same argument as in equation (18.12) is \(2\pi rQ_{\mathrm{r}} + \int_0^r q\,2\pi s\,\mathrm{d}s + P = 0\), so \(c_4 = P/(8\pi D)\). Without the force \(c_4 = 0\).
  7. For item 3: in steps 4 and 5 all terms of the derivative \(w'\) except \(c_3/r\) tend to zero as \(r \to 0\): \(K' = H/r = O(r^3)\), \(c_2r \to 0\) and \((r^2\ln r)' = 2r\ln r + r \to 0\). Since \(w\) is continuously differentiable in \(x\) and \(y\) and \(w(x, 0) = F(|x|)\) is an even function of \(x\), we have \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, 0) = 0\) and hence \(F'(r) = w_{\mathrm{x}}(r, 0) \to 0\). The term \(c_3/r\) with \(c_3 \ne 0\) is not bounded, so \(c_3 = 0\).

Source: EP (p. 406, equations (7.2.39) to (7.2.43)) obtains the same general solution by successive integrations and says that symmetry at the centre requires \(c_3 = 0\). VK (PDF p. 105) says that the logarithmic terms in a full plate without a point force give an infinite displacement, moment and shear force, so these constants are zero. The proof with the equilibrium of the disc for \(c_4\) and with the derivative for \(c_3\) is not from the source.

The theorem said two things: the plate equation for an \(r\)-dependent load is solved with four constants, and two of them vanish if the plate is whole and has no point force. Each hypothesis has its role. Without the continuity of the derivative at the centre the constant \(c_3\) would remain, and the plate would have a hole or a peak. Without the condition on the point force \(c_4\) remains, which we will see right away in the last lemma.

Now we can solve the example. We determine \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) from the boundary conditions at \(r = a\) (definition 18.19), first for a clamped edge, where \(w = 0\) and \(\partial w/\partial r = 0\).

Corollary 18.36 A clamped circular plate (vpeta krožna plošča)

A circular plate of radius \(a\) with a clamped edge, \(w(a) = 0\) and \(w'(a) = 0\), loaded by a uniform pressure \(q\), has

\[w = \frac{q\,(a^2 - r^2)^2}{64D} , \qquad w(0) = \frac{q a^4}{64D} , \tag{18.41}\]
\[M_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{q}{16}\,\big((3+\nu)\,r^2 - (1+\nu)\,a^2\big) , \qquad M_\theta = \frac{q}{16}\,\big((1+3\nu)\,r^2 - (1+\nu)\,a^2\big) , \qquad Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -\frac{qr}{2} . \tag{18.42}\]

The largest absolute value of the moments is at the edge, \(M_{\mathrm{r}}(a) = qa^2/8\). There \(M_\theta(a) = \nu\,qa^2/8\).

Proof

We must show that the function of theorem 18.35 with two constants satisfies both conditions at the edge.

  1. By item 3 of theorem 18.35, \(w = qr^4/(64D) + c_1 + c_2r^2\), since there is no point force at the centre and the plate is whole.
  2. The derivative is \(w' = qr^3/(16D) + 2c_2r\). The condition \(w'(a) = 0\) gives \(c_2 = -qa^2/(32D)\).
  3. The condition \(w(a) = 0\) gives \(c_1 = -qa^4/(64D) - c_2a^2 = qa^4/(64D)\).
  4. Substituting: \(w = \frac{q}{64D}(r^4 - 2a^2r^2 + a^4) = \frac{q}{64D}(a^2 - r^2)^2\). This is equation (18.41).
  5. Derivatives: \(w' = qr(r^2 - a^2)/(16D)\) and \(w'' = q(3r^2 - a^2)/(16D)\). Equations (18.39) give \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{q}{16}\big((3r^2 - a^2) + \nu(r^2 - a^2)\big)\) and \(M_\theta = \frac{q}{16}\big((r^2 - a^2) + \nu(3r^2 - a^2)\big)\), which is (18.42).
  6. \(Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -D(\nabla^2 w)'\), \(\nabla^2 w = q(2r^2 - a^2)/(8D)\) and \((\nabla^2 w)' = qr/(2D)\).
  7. At the edge \(r = a\) we have \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac q{16}(3 + \nu - 1 - \nu)a^2 = qa^2/8\) and \(M_\theta = \frac q{16}(1 + 3\nu - 1 - \nu)a^2 = \nu qa^2/8\).

Source: EP Example 7.2.1 (pp. 407-408) solves the same problem with the same constants and states that the largest moment is at the clamped edge. VK (PDF p. 106) gives the clamped edge under uniform load in equation (4.26) and the following. The notation with item 3 of the theorem and the steps are ours.

Let us look at the numbers for our plate (\(a = 250\) mm, \(q = 10\) kPa, \(D = 17\,948{,}7\) N m), computed in outlines/ch-plosce/num-06.py. The central deflection is \(w(0) = qa^4/(64D) = 0{,}03401\) mm, which is \(0{,}34\ \%\) of the thickness. At the edge \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = qa^2/8 = 78{,}13\) N m/m and at the centre \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = M_\theta = -(1+\nu)\,qa^2/16 = -50{,}78\) N m/m. At the edge the top surface is stretched, at the centre compressed, so the two moments have opposite signs. By corollary 18.8 the stress is \(\sigma_{\max} = 6|M|/h^2\), so \(4{,}69\) MPa at the edge and \(3{,}05\) MPa at the centre. The shear force \(Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -qr/2\) is \(-1250\) N/m at the edge, and the rim gives a total of \(2\pi a\cdot 1250 = 1963{,}5\) N, which is exactly the pressure \(q\) times the area \(\pi a^2\), as it must be by the equilibrium of the whole plate. Why is \(M_\theta(a) = \nu M_{\mathrm{r}}(a)\)? Because the edge is clamped, \(w'(a) = 0\) and the curvature in the circumferential direction \(w'/r\) is zero there, and from equations (18.39) it follows that \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = Dw''\) and \(M_\theta = \nu Dw''\). For a plate in the form of a strip the curvature in one direction is zero for another reason, but the result is the same: \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = \nu M_{\mathrm{x}}\) (section 18.4).

Now a simply supported edge, where \(w = 0\) and \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) (definition 18.19). This edge is circular and therefore smooth: unlike the square there are no corners on which a force \(2M_{\mathrm{xy}}\) would act (corollary 18.22), and because of \(M_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) (lemma 18.34) the effective shear force at the edge is simply \(Q_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Corollary 18.37 A simply supported circular plate (prosto podprta krožna plošča)

A circular plate of radius \(a\) with a simply supported edge, \(w(a) = 0\) and \(M_{\mathrm{r}}(a) = 0\), loaded by a uniform pressure \(q\), has

\[w = \frac{q\,(a^2 - r^2)}{64D}\Big(\frac{5+\nu}{1+\nu}\,a^2 - r^2\Big) , \qquad w(0) = \frac{5+\nu}{1+\nu}\,\frac{qa^4}{64D} , \tag{18.43}\]
\[M_{\mathrm{r}} = -\frac{(3+\nu)\,q}{16}\,(a^2 - r^2) , \qquad M_\theta = -\frac q{16}\big((3+\nu)\,a^2 - (1+3\nu)\,r^2\big) , \qquad Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -\frac{qr}2 . \tag{18.44}\]

The largest absolute value of both moments is at the centre, \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = M_\theta = -(3+\nu)\,qa^2/16\). The difference of the displacements of the supported and the clamped plate is the displacement caused by a uniform moment \(M_{\mathrm{a}} = -qa^2/8\) along the edge:

\[w_{\mathrm{podprta}} - w_{\mathrm{vpeta}} = -\frac{M_{\mathrm{a}}\,(a^2 - r^2)}{2D(1+\nu)} , \qquad M_{\mathrm{r}} = M_\theta = M_{\mathrm{a}} . \tag{18.45}\]
Proof

We must show that the function of theorem 18.35 with two constants satisfies both conditions and that the difference from the clamped plate is a field with a constant moment.

  1. By item 3 of theorem 18.35, \(w = qr^4/(64D) + c_1 + c_2r^2\), \(w' = qr^3/(16D) + 2c_2r\), \(w'' = 3qr^2/(16D) + 2c_2\).
  2. By equation (18.39) the condition \(M_{\mathrm{r}}(a) = 0\) is \(w''(a) + \nu w'(a)/a = 0\), that is \(\frac{(3+\nu)\,qa^2}{16D} + 2(1+\nu)c_2 = 0\), so \(c_2 = -\frac{(3+\nu)\,qa^2}{32(1+\nu)D}\).
  3. The condition \(w(a) = 0\) gives \(c_1 = -\frac{qa^4}{64D} - c_2a^2 = \frac{qa^4}{64D}\cdot\frac{5+\nu}{1+\nu}\).
  4. By substitution \(w = \frac{q}{64D}\Big(r^4 - \frac{2(3+\nu)}{1+\nu}a^2r^2 + \frac{5+\nu}{1+\nu}a^4\Big)\). The product in (18.43) is the same polynomial: the coefficient at \(a^2r^2\) is \(-1 - \frac{5+\nu}{1+\nu} = -\frac{2(3+\nu)}{1+\nu}\).
  5. Moments from equations (18.39): \(w'/r = qr^2/(16D) + 2c_2\), so \(w'' + \nu w'/r = \frac{(3+\nu)\,qr^2}{16D} + 2(1+\nu)\,c_2 = \frac{(3+\nu)\,q}{16D}\,(r^2 - a^2)\) with \(c_2\) from step 2, and \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = D(w'' + \nu w'/r) = -\frac{(3+\nu)q}{16}(a^2 - r^2)\). \(M_\theta\) follows in the same way from \(w'/r + \nu w''\). The shear force is the same as for the clamped plate (\(\nabla^2 w\) differs only by a constant, the derivative does not).
  6. For equation (18.45): the difference is \(w_{\mathrm{podprta}} - w_{\mathrm{vpeta}} = \frac{qa^2(a^2 - r^2)}{16(1+\nu)D}\) (we subtract the polynomials). The field \(c\,(a^2 - r^2)\) has \(w'' = -2c\) and \(w'/r = -2c\), so by equations (18.39) \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = M_\theta = -2cD(1+\nu)\). With \(c = -\frac{M_{\mathrm{a}}}{2D(1+\nu)}\) this is \(M_{\mathrm{a}}\), and for \(M_{\mathrm{a}} = -qa^2/8\) we get \(c = \frac{qa^2}{16(1+\nu)D}\).

Source: EP (p. 405, table 7.2.1) lists the conditions for a simply supported edge (\(w = 0\), \(M_{\mathrm{rr}} = M_{\mathrm{a}}\)) and VK (PDF pp. 105-106, equations (4.24) to (4.28)) solves the same problem with constants \(C_3\), \(C_4\). The difference as a constant moment (step 6) is not from the source.

The numbers for our plate: \(w(0) = 0{,}13864\) mm, which is \(1{,}4\ \%\) of the thickness (where the Kirchhoff assumption of a small deflection \(w \ll h\) still holds well), and at the centre \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = M_\theta = -128{,}91\) N m/m, which is a stress of \(7{,}73\) MPa. The ratio of the deflections \(0{,}13864/0{,}03401 = 4{,}077\) equals \((5+\nu)/(1+\nu)\).

Figure 18.18 shows where the ratio comes from. On the left is the section through the centre from edge to edge, the displacement drawn downward. For the clamped plate the displacement at the centre is \(0{,}0156\) (in units of \(qa^4/D\)), the clamped curve is blue, the supported curve is blackwhite and reaches \(0{,}0637\). Their difference is the dashed orange curve and is exactly the displacement under a constant edge moment \(M_{\mathrm{a}}\) from equation (18.45): \(0{,}0481\) at the centre, \(0{,}0156 + 0{,}0481 = 0{,}0637\). A simply supported plate is thus a clamped plate from which we take the clamping away: the moment \(qa^2/8\) that the clamping exerted at the edge is replaced by zero, that is we add the moment \(-qa^2/8\). On the right this is seen in the moments. The vertical axis carries \(-M_{\mathrm{r}}\), so that bending in the direction of the load is upward, and the values are in units of \(qa^2\). The clamped moment goes from \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = -0{,}0813\) at the centre to \(0{,}125\) at the edge, the simply supported one from \(-0{,}2063\) to \(0\), and the two curves are separated by the constant value \(0{,}125 = 1/8\). For \(\nu = 0\) the ratio \((5+\nu)/(1+\nu)\) is exactly \(5\), as for the beam with the ratio \(5qL^4/(384EI)\) to \(qL^4/(384EI)\) (section 18.4).

What does this mean in practice? VK (PDF p. 110) says that the true support lies between the two extremes and that it is sensible to compute both. For us they give: a deflection between \(0{,}034\) and \(0{,}139\) mm, a stress between \(4{,}69\) MPa (clamped, at the edge) and \(7{,}73\) MPa (supported, at the centre). The simply supported plate therefore has a \(4{,}08\) times larger deflection and a \(1{,}65\) times larger stress. Clamping is therefore most valuable for the deformation and less for the stress.

Example 18.38 A circle in a square (krog v kvadratu)

We compare the circular plate \(a = 250\) mm with the square plate \(500\) mm × \(500\) mm of section 18.5, of the same thickness \(h = 10\) mm and the same pressure \(q = 10\) kPa. Both are simply supported. The square has the central deflection \(0{,}1414\) mm, the circle \(0{,}1386\) mm. The ratio is \(0{,}980\): the circle has \(\pi/4 = 78{,}5\ \%\) of the area of the square, but only a \(2\ \%\) smaller deflection. For the clamped edge the deflection of the circle is \(0{,}0340\) mm, that of the square by Ritz's method (chapter 6, the number is from a later section of this chapter) \(0{,}0440\) mm, the ratio \(0{,}772\). Why the square and the inscribed circle have almost the same deflection for the simple support, we cannot show in one step: this is an observation from comparing numbers, not a theorem.

Let us return to the hypothesis on the point force. So far the load was a function \(q(r)\), which means that the force on every piece was smaller than the full force. What if the plate is loaded by a force \(P\) at one point, the centre? A point force is an idealization: in reality it acts on a small circle, and in the model there is nothing on it. Theorem 18.35 (item 2) predicts that the constant \(c_4\) will not be zero. Let us solve.

Lemma 18.39 A point force at the centre of a circular plate (točkovna sila v središču krožne plošče)

Let a clamped circular plate of radius \(a\) have a point force \(P\) in the direction of \(w\) at the centre and no load elsewhere. For \(0 < r \le a\),

\[w = \frac{P}{16\pi D}\Big(a^2 - r^2 + 2r^2\ln\frac ra\Big) , \qquad w(0) = \frac{Pa^2}{16\pi D} , \tag{18.46}\]
\[M_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac P{4\pi}\Big(1 - (1+\nu)\ln\frac ar\Big) , \qquad M_\theta = \frac P{4\pi}\Big(\nu - (1+\nu)\ln\frac ar\Big) , \qquad 2\pi r\,Q_{\mathrm{r}} = -P . \tag{18.47}\]

The displacement at the centre is finite, but the absolute values of the moments grow beyond all bounds as \(r \to 0\), like \(\ln(a/r)\).

Proof

We must show which term of the general solution remains and what happens to the derivatives.

  1. A point force \(P\) at the centre: by item 2 of theorem 18.35, \(c_4 = P/(8\pi D)\). The centre is smooth, so by item 3, \(c_3 = 0\). There is no load outside the centre, so \(w_{\mathrm{p}} = 0\) and \(w = c_1 + c_2r^2 + c_4r^2\ln r\).
  2. The derivative is \(w' = 2c_2r + c_4(2r\ln r + r)\). The condition \(w'(a) = 0\) gives \(c_2 = -c_4(2\ln a + 1)/2\).
  3. The condition \(w(a) = 0\) gives \(c_1 = -c_2a^2 - c_4a^2\ln a = c_4a^2/2\).
  4. Substituting: \(w = \frac{c_4}2\big(a^2 - r^2 + 2r^2\ln(r/a)\big)\) and \(c_4/2 = P/(16\pi D)\). This is equation (18.46). As \(r \to 0\) we have \(r^2\ln r \to 0\), so \(w(0) = Pa^2/(16\pi D)\).
  5. Derivatives: \(w' = \frac{P}{4\pi D}\,r\ln(r/a)\) and \(w'' = \frac P{4\pi D}\big(\ln(r/a) + 1\big)\). Equations (18.39) give \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{P}{4\pi}\big((1+\nu)\ln(r/a) + 1\big)\) and \(M_\theta = \frac P{4\pi}\big((1+\nu)\ln(r/a) + \nu\big)\), which is (18.47).
  6. \(\ln(a/r) \to \infty\) as \(r \to 0\), so \(M_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(M_\theta\) fall below all bounds, and their absolute values grow without bound. From item 2 of theorem 18.35 it follows that \(2\pi rQ_{\mathrm{r}} = -P\), which is the equilibrium of a disc with the force \(P\).

Source: EP Example 7.2.1(b) (pp. 407-408) gives the same solution for a point force on a clamped plate. RPS (PDF p. 190, equations (5.3.54) and (5.3.55)) solves the same problem for a simply supported edge. The proof with theorem 18.35 is ours.

Numbers for \(P = 1\) kN: \(w(0) = 0{,}06928\) mm, at the edge \(M_{\mathrm{r}} = P/(4\pi) = 79{,}6\) N m/m. The moment \(M_{\mathrm{r}}\) at a distance \(r\) from the centre is \(-86{,}9\), \(-253{,}4\), \(-491{,}6\) and \(-729{,}8\) N m/m at \(r = 50\), \(10\), \(1\) and \(0{,}1\) mm, which is a stress of \(5{,}22\), \(15{,}21\), \(29{,}50\) and \(43{,}79\) MPa (figure 18.19). The figure has \(r\) on the horizontal axis in a logarithmic scale, and \(-M_{\mathrm{r}}\), bending in the direction of the load, on the vertical one. Since \(-M_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a linear function of \(\ln(a/r)\), the graph is a straight line, and every tenfold decrease of \(r\) adds \(P(1+\nu)\ln 10/(4\pi) = 238{,}2\) N m/m to \(-M_{\mathrm{r}}\) (the points lie on the same line). At the edge \(-M_{\mathrm{r}} = -79{,}6\) N m/m. The plate thickness \(h\) is at \(r = 10\) mm, and the orange segment shows the distances smaller than it.

May we believe such numbers? Not always. A point force is not real, and the Kirchhoff plate (definition 18.2) is not a model for distances smaller than the thickness either, since there the normals do not stay straight with such a fast change of deflection. The distance at which the model still holds must be larger than \(h\), so \(r > 10\) mm: the stresses \(29{,}50\) MPa at \(r = 1\) mm and \(43{,}79\) MPa at \(r = 0{,}1\) mm are a consequence of the model and not a prediction for a real steel plate. EP (p. 406) therefore prescribes, after Nadai and Westergaard, that the largest moment under a point force on a small circle be computed with an equivalent radius \(r_{\mathrm{e}}\) that depends on \(h\). The energy stays finite: the energy (definition 18.14) contains \((\nabla^2 w)^2\), so a term of order \(\ln^2 r\), and the integral \(\int_0^a r\ln^2 r\,\mathrm{d}r\) is finite. Hence a point force is, in the energy sense, an admissible load, in spite of the infinite moment at one point.

We have seen how the circle is a special shape that demands only an ordinary equation. The clamped and the simply supported plate are two extremes of the true support, the difference between them is one edge moment, and the point force is a case where the hypothesis of the theorem does not hold and the logarithm remains. For the square (section 18.5) we therefore needed a series, for the circle only four integrals. What remained unsolved is a plate that is not full: an annular plate with a hole has all four constants \(c_1\) to \(c_4\) and EP treats it with a table of boundary conditions (EP, p. 405), we do not compute it. The buckling of a circular plate we cite and do not prove (EP, pp. 411-414, section 7.2.2.2).

18.7 Energy methods for plates

So far we have solved the plate with the equation \(D\nabla^4 w = q\) (theorem 18.12) and with series whose terms satisfy the edge conditions by themselves: the double sine series for the simply supported rectangle (theorem 18.30) and a polynomial in \(r\) for the circle (theorem 18.35). Already a square clamped along its whole edge has no such solution. Timoshenko says of the plate with all four edges built in that its treatment meets many difficulties, and that the first solution usable for numerical computation was given by Kojalovich (TIMO, PDF p. 348). What do we do when no series fits the supports? We use the same energies that we used for the beam in chapters 6, 8 and 13. The section has four parts. First the Ritz method for the clamped square. Then Hamilton's principle for the plate, and from it the shapes of vibration of the simply supported rectangle, which we call modes (načini) because each of them is one way in which the plate can vibrate as a whole with a single frequency. Then the Rayleigh quotient, which estimates the lowest frequency without solving the equation. Finally buckling (uklon): the compressive force in the plane of the plate at which the flat state is replaced by a curved one, the same phenomenon as for the column (chapter 8). The model is the same in all four as in section 18.1: a thin plate (definition 18.1) with constant \(D\) and thickness \(h\), small deflections and ideal supports.

18.7.1 Admissible fields and the energy form

For the beam, the Ritz method looked for the smallest total potential energy among the fields that satisfy the geometric conditions (definition 6.32, theorem 6.34). For the plate the potential of the load is \(-\int_\Omega q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\) and the energy is \(U\) of definition 18.14. The total potential energy is

\[\Pi(w) = U(w) - \int_\Omega q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A , \qquad U(w) = \tfrac12\,B(w, w) , \tag{18.48}\]

where \(B\) is the symmetric bilinear form

\[B(v, w) = D\int_\Omega \Big[\nabla^2 v\,\nabla^2 w - (1 - \nu)\big(v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{yy}} + v_{\mathrm{yy}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - 2\,v_{\mathrm{xy}}\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}\big)\Big]\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{18.49}\]

At \(v = w\) it is twice the energy of definition 18.14. The mass form is \(\mathcal{M}(v, w) = \rho h\int_\Omega v\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\), where \(\rho h\) is the mass of the plate per unit area of the middle plane. The fields that the energy accepts are defined as follows.

Definition 18.40 Admissible field of a plate (dopustno polje plošče)

Let \(\Omega = [0, a] \times [0, b]\) be the middle plane of a plate (definition 18.1). An admissible field (dopustno polje) is a function \(v : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) that satisfies two conditions.

  1. The function \(v\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(\Omega\), so that all terms of the integral (18.49) are continuous and the integral exists.
  2. The field satisfies the geometric boundary conditions (geometrijski robni pogoji) of definition 18.19: \(v = 0\) on every clamped or simply supported edge and \(\partial v/\partial n = 0\) on every clamped edge.

The conditions for moment and shear force on the edge (natural conditions) are not required of an admissible field. A trial space (definition 6.32) all of whose fields are admissible is conforming (skladen).

Source: The definition is ours, after definition 13.49. EP §7.2.6 (p. 455) takes the approximating functions as products of one-dimensional functions that satisfy the geometric conditions.

The Gaussian curvature \(v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}} - v_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\) enters the energy because a plate bends in two directions at once, and in (18.49) it is carried by the term with the factor \(1 - \nu\). The next lemma says that on a rectangle where the field is zero on the edge this term vanishes from the integral. It need not be computed, which simplifies all calculations in this section.

Lemma 18.41 The curvature term on a rectangle is zero (Gaussov člen pri pravokotniku je nič)

Let \(v\) be three times continuously differentiable on \(\Omega = [0, a] \times [0, b]\) and \(v = 0\) on all four edges. Then

\[\int_\Omega \big(v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}} - v_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}A = 0 , \tag{18.50}\]

and so \(B(v, v) = D\int_\Omega (\nabla^2 v)^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), and by polarization \(B(v, w) = D\int_\Omega \nabla^2 v\,\nabla^2 w\,\mathrm{d}A\) for two such fields.

Proof

We must show that the integrand is the divergence of a field and that its flux through the edge is zero.

  1. We have \(\partial_{\mathrm{x}}(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}}) - \partial_{\mathrm{y}}(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{xy}}) = v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}} + v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{xyy}} - v_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 - v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{xyy}} = v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}} - v_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\). The mixed derivatives agree because the derivatives up to third order are continuous.
  2. The plane divergence theorem (theorem 4.14) for the field \((v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}},\, -v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{xy}})\) on the rectangle says that the integral equals \(\oint (v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} - v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}})\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  3. On the edges \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \pm 1\), leaving \(\pm v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}}\). On the edge \(v(0, y) = 0\) for every \(y\), so the second derivative along the edge is also zero: \(v_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). The term is zero.
  4. On the edges \(y = 0\) and \(y = b\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = \pm 1\), leaving \(\mp v_{\mathrm{x}}\,v_{\mathrm{xy}}\). On the edge \(v(x, 0) = 0\) for every \(x\), so \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) along the edge. The term is zero.
  5. Hence (18.50). The term with \((1 - \nu)\) in (18.49) at \(w = v\) is \(-2D(1 - \nu)\int (v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,v_{\mathrm{yy}} - v_{\mathrm{xy}}^2)\,\mathrm{d}A\), and it vanishes. For two fields \(v\), \(w\) we apply this to \(v + w\), \(v\) and \(w\): the bilinear expression \(v_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{yy}} + v_{\mathrm{yy}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - 2\,v_{\mathrm{xy}}\,w_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the polarization of the Gaussian expression, so its integral is zero.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. EP (pp. 431-434) has the result more generally: for a general edge the term gives only an edge integral, treated by theorem 18.21.

On a rectangle, clamping and simple support therefore give the same energy, because they differ only in the condition on the slope, which did not enter (18.50). The difference shows only in which fields are admissible. The Ritz method for the clamped square is the first test.

18.7.2 The Ritz method for the clamped square

Take a square of side \(a\), clamped along the whole edge and loaded uniformly by \(q\). The steel plate has \(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(h = 10\) mm, so \(D = 17\,948{,}7\) N m, and \(a = 500\) mm, \(q = 10\) kPa, as in the example of the square in section 18.5. The trial fields must be zero and have zero slope on the edge. The polynomial \((1 - \xi^2)^2(1 - \eta^2)^2\) in the dimensionless coordinates \(\xi = 2x/a - 1\), \(\eta = 2y/a - 1\) from \([-1, 1]^2\) does this, since it has a double zero on every edge (\(\xi = \pm 1\) or \(\eta = \pm 1\)). The plate and the trial fields are symmetric about both midlines, so we also take products with \(\xi^{2i}\eta^{2j}\).

Theorem 18.42 Ritz method for a clamped rectangular plate (Ritzova metoda za vpeto pravokotno ploščo)

Let the plate be a rectangle \(\Omega\) clamped along the whole edge, with constant \(D\) and continuous load \(q\). Let \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{\mathrm{N}}\) be linearly independent polynomials with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{p}} = 0\) and \(\partial\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}/\partial n = 0\) on the edge, and \(K_{\mathrm{ps}} = B(\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{s}})\), \(f_{\mathrm{p}} = \int_\Omega q\,\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\,\mathrm{d}A\). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric and positive definite, \(K_{\mathrm{ps}} = D\int_\Omega \nabla^2\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\,\nabla^2\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}A\).
  2. The field \(w_{\mathrm{N}} = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} c_{\mathrm{p}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\) has the smallest value of \(\Pi\) among all fields of the trial space exactly when \(\mat K\,\vek c = \vek f\).
  3. The work of the load on the Ritz field is \(\int_\Omega q\,w_{\mathrm{N}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek c\cdot\vek f\), and it is not larger than the work on the true solution \(w\), if one exists. For nested trial spaces this work does not decrease with \(N\).
Proof

We must show that the clamped field fits lemma 18.41, that \(\Pi\) is a quadratic function with a definite matrix on the trial space, and that theorem 6.34 then applies.

  1. The fields \(\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\) are zero on the edge, so by lemma 18.41 \(K_{\mathrm{ps}} = D\int\nabla^2\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\,\nabla^2\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}A\). Symmetry follows from the symmetry of the product.
  2. Let \(v = \sum c_{\mathrm{p}}\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\vek c^\T\mat K\,\vek c = D\int(\nabla^2 v)^2\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\). The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, hence zero everywhere (lemma 3.39): \(\nabla^2 v = 0\). Theorem 4.14 for the field \(v\,\nabla v\) gives \(\int|\nabla v|^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \oint v\,\partial v/\partial n\,\mathrm{d}s - \int v\,\nabla^2 v\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), because \(v = 0\) on the edge. Again a continuous nonnegative integrand: \(\nabla v = 0\), so \(v\) is constant and by the edge condition zero. Independence of the fields gives \(\vek c = \vek 0\). The matrix is therefore positive definite.
  3. The potential is \(\Pi(v) = \tfrac12\,\vek c^\T\mat K\,\vek c - \vek c\cdot\vek f\). At \(\mat K\,\vek c^* = \vek f\) we have \(\Pi = \Pi^* + \tfrac12(\vek c - \vek c^*)^\T\mat K(\vek c - \vek c^*)\) with \(\Pi^* = -\tfrac12\,\vek c^*\cdot\vek f\) (expanding the square, symmetry of \(\mat K\)). By step 2 the second term is positive except at \(\vek c = \vek c^*\). This is point 2.
  4. The work is \(\int q\,w_{\mathrm{N}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \sum c_{\mathrm{p}} f_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek c^*\cdot\vek f\) and \(\Pi(w_{\mathrm{N}}) = -\tfrac12\,\vek c^*\cdot\vek f\). The true \(w\) satisfies the weak form \(B(w, \varphi) = \int q\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}A\) for every clamped field \(\varphi\) (theorem 18.21), and clamped fields have zero essential conditions. By point 2 of theorem 6.34, \(\int q\,w_{\mathrm{N}}\,\mathrm{d}A \le \int q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\). If the first space is contained in the second, the second space also contains the Ritz field of the first, so the smallest value of \(\Pi\) on the second space (point 2) is at most as large as on the first. Since \(\Pi(w_{\mathrm{N}})\) is minus half the work, the work does not decrease.

Source: EP §7.2.6 (pp. 455-461), examples with functions that satisfy the geometric conditions. The proof in steps is not from the sources, it follows theorem 6.34. Existence of the solution \(w\) is assumed and not proved (EP).

Figure 18.20 shows the computation by theorem 18.42. We draw the midline \(y = a/2\) of the clamped square, the \(x\) axis horizontal and the deflection \(w\) downward, in the direction of the load, at the scale \(10^{-3}\,q a^4/D\) per centimetre. At the left and right edges is the clamping, two vertical hatched lines, where \(w = 0\) and the slope is zero. With one term \(c\,(1 - \xi^2)^2(1 - \eta^2)^2\) we have \(K = 65\,536/1225\) and \(f = 256/225\) in the units of \(\xi\), \(\eta\) (integrals over \([-1, 1]^2\)), so \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 49/36\,864\ q a^4/D = 0{,}001329\ q a^4/D\). With ten terms (\(i + j \le 3\)) the curve is hard to tell from the first on the figure, and has \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}001265\ q a^4/D\). Both are blue because both are admissible, and they lie close together. At \(a = 500\) mm and \(q = 10\) kPa, \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}0440\) mm with ten terms and \(0{,}0463\) mm with one. The simply supported plate in section 18.5 had \(0{,}1415\) mm, which is \(3{,}2\) times more. Clamping is an additional constraint that prevents rotation of the edge, and a constraint makes the plate stiffer. The strip in section 18.4 showed the same: clamping gives five times smaller deflection than simple support (\(0{,}0907\) against \(0{,}4534\) mm).

We first draw the \(x\) axis and the \(w\) axis along the midline. The plate is clamped at both edges, where the deflection is zero and so is the slope, so the curves enter there horizontally. The Ritz approximation with one term matches the shape of the plate: largest in the middle and falling toward the edges with zero slope. The Ritz approximation with ten terms lies beside it, because the first term stayed the main one. The orange curve is the same computation with another trial field, which we explain below.

The table shows how the result changes with \(N\) (trial fields \(i + j \le K\), \(N = 1, 3, 6, 10\) for \(K = 0, 1, 2, 3\), SymPy and NumPy, outlines/ch-plosce/num-07.out). The work of the load \(\int q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\) is \(q\int w\,\mathrm{d}A\), so the table lists \(\int w\,\mathrm{d}A\) in units of \(q a^6/D\).

\(N\) \(w_{\mathrm{c}}\ [q a^4/D]\) \(\int w\,\mathrm{d}A\ [q a^6/D]\)
1 \(0{,}001329\) \(0{,}0003781\)
3 \(0{,}001263\) \(0{,}0003889\)
6 \(0{,}001265\) \(0{,}0003891\)
10 \(0{,}001265\) \(0{,}0003891\)

The work column grows, as point 3 of theorem 18.42 says. The \(w_{\mathrm{c}}\) column does not: it falls from one term to three, then rises slightly. The theorem bounds the work, not the central deflection, because the work \(\int q\,w\,\mathrm{d}A\) is a global measure of compliance, while the deflection at one point can be distorted by the error around that point in either direction. EP (p. 461) gives \(0{,}00134\) and \(0{,}00133\) for two choices of a single function and \(0{,}00126\) as the »exact« value, quoted from Timoshenko and Woinowsky-Krieger, which agrees with our ten-term \(0{,}001265\) to the digits printed. By »exact« EP means a value from a series and not from a closed form, so we do not repeat it here as a result of this book. Convergence \(w_{\mathrm{N}} \to w\) would follow from theorem 6.35 if the family is dense in the energy norm. We do not prove this density here (EP §6.3.3 lists the requirements for the choice of functions). The numbers show that the values settle at four digits.

What if the field is not admissible? Take the field \(x(a - x)\,y(a - y)\), which is zero on the edge but has a nonzero slope there. It is admissible for the simply supported plate, but not for the clamped one. Lemma 18.41 holds for it, since it is zero on the edge, and \(B(v, v)\) does not contain \(\nu\). Steps 1 to 3 of the proof of theorem 18.42 use only \(v = 0\) on the edge, not the slope, so the same procedure gives \(c = f/B\) with \(f = a^4/36\) and \(B = (22/45)\,D\) (units with \(a = 1\)), hence \(w_{\mathrm{c}} = 0{,}003551\ q a^4/D\) and work \(0{,}001578\ q a^6/D\) (outlines/ch-plosce/num-07.out, part B). This is four times more work than with ten admissible terms and about three times more deflection than the true clamped plate. The reason is in step 4: theorem 6.34 requires the difference \(e = w - w_{\mathrm{N}}\) to be a test function with zero essential conditions, but here \(e\) has a slope on the edge and is not a test function. The trial space is here wider than the clamped fields, hence softer, and it finds the minimum of \(\Pi\) for another problem: a plate whose edge may rotate. The value \(0{,}003551\) is an approximation for the simply supported plate (Navier, section 18.5, \(0{,}004062\)), not for the clamped one.

18.7.3 The plate in motion: Hamilton's principle

For the beam, Hamilton's principle (theorem 13.28) gave the equation of motion and the edge conditions from the stationarity of a single action. The same procedure works for the plate. The kinetic energy of the plate is \(T = \tfrac12\int_\Omega\rho h\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), because a piece of the middle plane of area \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) has mass \(\rho h A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\). This neglects the rotatory inertia of the normal, as for the beam. How good is that? Rotatory inertia adds to the term \(\rho h\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\) the term \(\tfrac{\rho h^3}{12}(w_{\mathrm{xt}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{yt}}^2)\). For a shape with wave number \(k\) the ratio is \(k^2h^2/12\) (as for the beam, section 13.5.1). The first mode of the simply supported square has \(k^2 = 2\pi^2/a^2\), so at \(a = 500\) mm, \(h = 10\) mm the ratio is \(6{,}6\cdot 10^{-4}\), and it stays below \(10^{-2}\) as long as \(k\,h < 0{,}34\) (\(0{,}34^2/12 = 0{,}0096\)), that is a wavelength \(2\pi/k\) longer than \(18{,}5\,h\).

Definition 18.43 Action of a plate (akcija plošče)

Let \(\Omega = [0, a]\times[0, b]\) be a plate with constant \(D\) and \(\rho h\), without edge loads, and let \([t_1, t_2]\) be a time interval. The action (definition 8.101) of a field \(w : \Omega\times[t_1, t_2] \to \mathbb{R}\) is

\[\mathcal{S}(w) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2}\Big(\tfrac12\rho h\int_\Omega w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}A - \Pi(w(\cdot, t))\Big)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{18.51}\]

where \(\Pi\) is the potential (18.48). The field \(w\) is admissible if \(w\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and all derivatives of \(w\) in \(x\), \(y\) up to fourth order are continuous on \(\Omega\times[t_1, t_2]\) and \(w(\cdot, t)\) is an admissible field of the plate (definition 18.40) at every \(t\). An admissible variation \(\eta\) is a continuously differentiable function whose derivatives \(\eta_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{yy}}\) are continuous, which is zero at \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) and which satisfies on the edge the same geometric conditions as the field, but with zero (where \(w\) is prescribed, \(\eta = 0\), where the slope is prescribed, \(\partial\eta/\partial n = 0\)).

Source: After theorem 13.28, expressed with the energy of the plate. The definition is ours.
